### Qwen-Image's encoder is Qwen2.5-VL · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Qwen-Image's encoder is Qwen2.5-VL — a full VLM — deliberately chosen OVER T5 and over the plain Qwen3 LLM.**

The technical report gives three reasons: (1) Qwen2.5-VL's language and visual spaces are already aligned, making it better suited to T2I than language-only encoders like Qwen3; (2) it retains strong language-modeling ability without degradation; (3) its multimodal input unlocks editing. Conditioning is the last-layer hidden state (encoder_hidden_states.hidden_states[-1]) of the LLM backbone — NOT a pooled CLIP embedding and NOT T5's bidirectional encoder output. This is a causal, autoregressive read of your prompt, so word ORDER and grammatical structure carry real weight, unlike a CLIP bag-of-concepts.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Write Qwen-Image prompts as well-formed, ordered natural-language sentences, not comma-salad tags. Put the most important subject/composition facts FIRST — the causal LLM reads left-to-right and early tokens anchor the scene. Do not port an SDXL Danbooru tag string verbatim.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen-VL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Verbatim-confirmed by the Qwen-Image Technical Report (arXiv:2508.02324) via HF papers mirror: 'Qwen-Image employs the Qwen2.5-VL model as the feature extraction module for textual inputs' for three stated reasons — (1) 'The language and visual spaces of Qwen2.5-VL have already been aligned, which makes it more suitable for text-to-image tasks compared to language-based models like Qwen3'; (2) 'Qwen2.5-VL retains strong language modeling capabilities, without significant degradation'; (3) 'Qwen2.5-VL supports multimodal inputs... e.g., image editing.' Conditioning: 'we utilize the latent of the last layer's hidden state from Qwen2.5-VL language model backbone' — i.e. hidden_states[-1], confirmed in diffusers pipeline_qwenimage.py (encoder class Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration). Caveat: an older Qwen2-VL-era note describes a penultimate layer; the SHIPPED Qwen-Image uses the LAST layer, so the finding is correct. The left-to-right/early-token-anchoring prompt rule is a reasonable engineering inference from causal-LM conditioning, not a directly measured paper claim, but the architectural facts it rests on are confirmed.
- **Sources:** [Qwen-Image Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02324) (Qwen Team (Alibaba), 2025) — Qwen2.5-VL chosen as text encoder over T5/Qwen3 for three stated reasons (aligned vision-language space, retained language modeling, multimodal input); last-layer hidden state used as the conditioning representation. arXiv:2508.02324

### Qwen-Image's REAL token budget is huge vs CLIP/T5 · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Qwen-Image's REAL token budget is huge vs CLIP/T5: 1024-token hard ceiling, 512 default — roughly 13x CLIP's 77 and 2x FLUX-dev's T5 512.**

tokenizer_max_length=1024 is the hard cap; the __call__ default max_sequence_length=512. About 34 tokens are consumed by the (stripped) system span. Compare: CLIP-L/bigG truncate hard at 77 tokens (ComfyUI fakes longer prompts by chunking into 75-token blocks and concatenating); FLUX/Chroma's T5-XXL caps at 512 (256 on Schnell). So Qwen-Image genuinely ingests paragraph-length prompts in one coherent causal pass, with no chunk seams.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** You can safely write 2-4 sentence prompts for Qwen-Image (aim under ~480 tokens / ~1900 English chars to stay inside the 512 default; raise max_sequence_length toward 1024 only if you genuinely need it). Stop translating CLIP-era brevity habits — but every token past the limit is silently dropped from the TAIL, so never bury the key subject at the end.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen-VL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: All numbers verified. diffusers pipeline_qwenimage.py: tokenizer_max_length=1024 (hard ceiling), default max_sequence_length=512. CLIP=77 (confirmed via FLUX encoder article + diffusers issue #2136), FLUX.1-dev T5-XXL=512 (256 on Schnell) confirmed. 1024/77 ≈ 13.3x and 512=512 (2x is the ceiling-vs-default framing: Qwen's 1024 hard cap is 2x FLUX-dev T5's 512 cap; Qwen's 512 DEFAULT equals FLUX-dev's 512 cap). The '2x FLUX-dev' phrasing is accurate only at the hard-ceiling level (1024 vs 512), not at the default level — minor but worth flagging. Tail-truncation warning (every token past the limit dropped from the tail) is correct given truncation=True. Prompt rule sound.
- **Sources:** [diffusers pipeline_qwenimage.py](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/main/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage.py) (Hugging Face, 2025) — tokenizer_max_length=1024 hard ceiling; max_sequence_length default 512 in __call__. ; [FLUX.1-dev: Encoders and Token Limitations](https://medium.com/@lbq999/flux-1-dev-encoders-and-token-limitations-8631c179eaad) (Boqiang Liang, 2024) — CLIP capped at 77 tokens; T5-XXL in FLUX capped at 512 (256 on Schnell) via max_sequence_length.

### Qwen-Image silently prepends a FIXED system prompt and… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Qwen-Image silently prepends a FIXED system prompt and strips its first 34 tokens before conditioning — the system prompt steers the LLM's read but never reaches the image.**

The diffusers pipeline wraps every prompt as: '<|im_start|>system\nDescribe the image by detailing the color, shape, size, texture, quantity, text, spatial relationships of the objects and background:<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user\n{}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n'. prompt_template_encode_start_idx=34 means the first 34 hidden states (the system span) are dropped; only the user-prompt + assistant hidden states condition the DiT. This is why Qwen-Image rewards prompts phrased as concrete visual DESCRIPTION (color/shape/size/texture/quantity/text/spatial) — the system prompt primes the LLM to extract exactly those axes.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Phrase prompts to answer the built-in system question: state color, shape, size, texture, COUNT, any on-image TEXT (in quotes), and spatial relationships explicitly. 'three brass lanterns, left-to-right, smallest in front' beats 'lanterns'. You do not need to (and cannot usefully) inject your own system prompt in standard pipelines — it is overwritten.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen-VL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Verbatim-confirmed in diffusers pipeline_qwenimage.py. System prompt: '<|im_start|>system\nDescribe the image by detailing the color, shape, size, texture, quantity, text, spatial relationships of the objects and background:<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user\n{}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n'. prompt_template_encode_start_idx=34 (template tokens dropped before conditioning), tokenizer_max_length=1024, default max_sequence_length=512, conditioning from hidden_states[-1]. The prompt rule (answer color/shape/size/texture/COUNT/on-image TEXT/spatial relations explicitly; cannot usefully inject your own system prompt in standard pipelines) follows directly from the hardcoded template and the strip behavior. Sound.
- **Sources:** [diffusers pipeline_qwenimage.py (QwenImagePipeline source)](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/main/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage.py) (Hugging Face, 2025) — Hardcoded system prompt template; prompt_template_encode_start_idx=34; tokenizer_max_length=1024; default max_sequence_length=512; conditioning from hidden_states[-1].

### Z-Image's encoder is Qwen3-4B · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Z-Image's encoder is Qwen3-4B — a pure LLM (no vision) — chosen for bilingual instruction-alignment and efficiency, with conditioning from the SECOND-to-last hidden layer (dim 2560).**

The Z-Image paper: 'we employ the lightweight Qwen3-4B as the text encoder, leveraging its bilingual proficiency to align complex instructions with visual content.' Reference code takes hidden_states[-2] (2560-dim) as conditioning — NOT the last layer (unlike Qwen-Image's hidden_states[-1]). Text and image tokens are concatenated into one S3-DiT stream but separated by 3D RoPE axes (text increments on the temporal axis, image on spatial), so text and image don't compete for positions.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Treat Z-Image like a small, literal instruction-follower: clear, declarative, bilingual-friendly natural language. It is a 4B LLM, not a frontier model — keep instructions concrete and unambiguous; don't rely on subtle world-knowledge or implication the way you might with a large chat model.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen3 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Encoder confirmed in Z-Image Technical Report (arXiv:2511.22699 html v2): 'we employ the lightweight Qwen3-4B as the text encoder, leveraging its bilingual proficiency to align complex instructions with visual content' — a pure LLM, no vision tower. The hidden_states[-2] / dim 2560 detail is NOT stated in the paper (paper does not disclose which layer); it is sourced from the strong-community fblissjr ComfyUI-QwenImageWanBridge z_image_encoder.md, which states 'Embedding Layer Used: hidden_states[-2] (second-to-last)' and 'Hidden Size: 2560.' So encoder identity and rationale are paper-grounded; the specific layer/dim is implementation-grounded (community, not paper). Net: CONFIRMED with the layer/dim caveat noted. Prompt rule (treat as a small literal 4B instruction-follower) is reasonable.
- **Sources:** [Z-Image: An Efficient Image Generation Foundation Model with Single-Stream Diffusion Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22699) (Tongyi-MAI (Alibaba), 2025) — Qwen3-4B used as text encoder for bilingual instruction-to-visual alignment; single-stream S3-DiT fuses text/visual/VAE tokens with 3D unified RoPE on separate axes. arXiv:2511.22699 ; [Z-Image Text Encoder (ComfyUI-QwenImageWanBridge docs)](https://github.com/fblissjr/ComfyUI-QwenImageWanBridge/blob/main/nodes/docs/z_image_encoder.md) (fblissjr, 2025) — Conditioning from hidden_states[-2], dim 2560; max_sequence_length=512 via truncation; axes_lens=[1536,512,512]; filter_padding=True by default.

### Z-Image wraps prompts in a chat template and can run a… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Z-Image wraps prompts in a chat template and can run a <think> reasoning block (enable_thinking) — reasoning/knowledge is offloaded to a SEPARATE Prompt Enhancer VLM, not the encoder.**

The reference template is '<|im_start|>user\n{}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n' (matching diffusers with enable_thinking=True default); an optional system block '<|im_start|>system\n{content}<|im_end|>' can be prepended. But the paper is explicit that heavy lifting is a module, not the encoder: 'we propose equipping Z-Image with a Prompt Enhancer (PE), powered by system prompt and a pretrained VLM, to improve its reasoning and knowledge capabilities.' So the raw Qwen3-4B encoder is NOT where you put a paragraph expecting reasoning — that's the PE's job.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** For Z-Image, either (a) let the official Prompt Enhancer expand a short seed concept, OR (b) feed an already-detailed, self-contained visual description — but do NOT hand the raw encoder a terse cryptic prompt and expect it to reason out the scene; it won't, the PE does. If you bypass the PE, write the full description yourself.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen3 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Separate Prompt Enhancer confirmed verbatim in Z-Image Technical Report (html v2): the PE is 'powered by system prompt and a pretrained VLM, to improve its reasoning and knowledge capabilities,' kept fixed during alignment, distinct from the Qwen3-4B encoder. Chat template + think-block confirmed in fblissjr docs: template '<|im_start|>user\n{}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n', add_think_block default True, <think></think> support via thinking_content. Nuance: the paper frames reasoning as happening in the PE BEFORE text reaches the model; the <think> block is a ComfyUI-node-level feature exposed on the encoder path. Both claims hold; the prompt rule (use the PE or write a full self-contained description; don't feed a terse cryptic prompt expecting the encoder to reason) is well-supported.
- **Sources:** [Z-Image Technical Report (arXiv:2511.22699)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22699v2) (Tongyi-MAI (Alibaba), 2025) — A separate Prompt Enhancer (PE), powered by a pretrained VLM + system prompt, supplies reasoning/knowledge — distinct from the Qwen3-4B encoder itself. arXiv:2511.22699 ; [Z-Image Text Encoder docs](https://github.com/fblissjr/ComfyUI-QwenImageWanBridge/blob/main/nodes/docs/z_image_encoder.md) (fblissjr, 2025) — Chat template '<|im_start|>user\n{}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n' with enable_thinking default; optional system block; supports <think>{reasoning}</think>.

## Depictability

### CLIP encodes concrete visual words robustly but… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CLIP encodes concrete visual words robustly but abstract/non-visual words inconsistently — the brittleness is word-TYPE-specific, not random.**

Karthik et al. show CLIP text encoders are 'brittle': semantically-equivalent paraphrases and reorderings produce divergent embeddings, AND the divergence is far larger for abstract/emotional/non-visual tokens than for concrete depictable nouns/adjectives. Concrete visual words (objects, colors, materials, observable actions) land in stable, well-separated regions of the embedding space; abstract words ('grief', 'guarded', 'regulation-issue') map to mushy, overlapping regions with no consistent visual referent, because CLIP's contrastive objective only ever rewarded text that matched pixels. An abstract token therefore contributes a near-arbitrary direction to the conditioning vector — it does not encode 'nothing', it encodes noise.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Every adjective/noun in the prompt must name something a camera could photograph. Replace 'worn by grief' → 'dark circles under eyes, downturned mouth, slumped shoulders'; 'guarded' → 'arms crossed, chin lowered, narrowed eyes'; 'regulation-issue jacket' → 'plain olive-drab jacket, brass buttons'. If you cannot point to the pixel it changes, cut the word.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed, but with a sourcing caveat the researcher should know. The headline finding of the named source 'On the Brittleness of CLIP Text Encoders' (arXiv:2511.04247) is that CLIP embeddings are unstable under paraphrase/reorder, with brittleness 'concentrated in trivial surface edits such as punctuation and case' and syntactic/semantic perturbations driving the largest instabilities. That abstract does NOT itself foreground a clean 'concrete-robust vs abstract-brittle' word-type split or token-dominance claim as stated. The word-TYPE-specific brittleness is real but is grounded by MECHANISM (Radford et al. 2021: CLIP's text space is shaped only by what contrastively discriminates 400M images, so non-visual text has no grounded target) and corroborated by the reporting-bias literature (finding 2's source). So the prompt_rule ('replace non-photographable words with photographable ones') is sound and well-grounded; just attribute the concrete-vs-abstract robustness gap to the grounding-mechanism + reporting-bias papers, not to 2511.04247's surface-edit result. The 'certain tokens disproportionately dominate the embedding' sub-claim is better supported by the attention-regulation paper (2403.06381) than by 2511.04247.
- **Sources:** [On the Brittleness of CLIP Text Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04247) (2025) — CLIP text encoders produce inconsistent embeddings under paraphrase/reorder, with concrete visual words encoded more robustly than abstract/non-visual words; certain tokens disproportionately dominate the final embedding. arXiv:2511.04247 ; [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (Radford et al., 2021) — CLIP is trained by contrastive image-caption matching on 400M pairs, so its text space is shaped only by what discriminates images — non-visual text has no grounded target. arXiv:2103.00020

### CLIP/OpenCLIP behave like a bag-of-words cross-modally · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CLIP/OpenCLIP behave like a bag-of-words cross-modally: they cannot reliably bind which adjective goes with which noun, so multi-attribute character prompts leak.**

Lin et al. prove CLIP matches 'orange square + blue triangle' to 'blue square + orange triangle' — the binding info exists unimodally but is lost in cross-modal cosine alignment. For SDXL (CLIP-L + bigG, both bag-of-words encoders), this means 'red scarf, green eyes, blue coat' frequently swaps colors across items. The more attributes you cram per noun, and the more competing nouns, the worse binding gets. Abstract/narrative tokens make it worse by adding ungrounded directions the U-Net must still attend to.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Bind tightly and order adjacency-first: put each attribute immediately before its noun ('crimson scarf, emerald eyes, navy coat'), one or two attributes per noun max. For SDXL specifically, keep distinct subjects few; if two characters need different colors, expect leakage and consider regional prompting / separate generations rather than one dense prompt.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed. 'CLIP Behaves like a Bag-of-Words Model Cross-modally but not Uni-modally' (arXiv:2502.03566): attribute-object binding IS encoded within CLIP's text and image embeddings unimodally but is lost in cross-modal alignment, producing bag-of-words attribute-swap failures. Important nuance the prompt_rule should reflect: the paper's punchline is that the binding info survives unimodally and can be recovered by a simple linear transform on text embeddings — i.e., the leakage is a cross-modal-alignment artifact, not a total absence of compositional structure. SDXL inheritance sub-claim confirmed: SDXL concatenates penultimate-layer token features from CLIP ViT-L/14 ([B,77,768]) and OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 ([B,77,1280]) → [B,77,2048] (Podell et al. 2023), both bag-of-words encoders, so the binding weakness carries over. Adjacency-first ordering and regional prompting are reasonable mitigations.
- **Sources:** [CLIP Behaves like a Bag-of-Words Model Cross-modally but not Uni-modally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03566) (2025) — Attribute-object binding is present in CLIP's unimodal embeddings but lost in cross-modal cosine alignment, causing systematic attribute-swap (bag-of-words) failures. arXiv:2502.03566 ; [SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01952) (Podell et al., 2023) — SDXL conditions on concatenated CLIP ViT-L/14 + OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 token features — both are bag-of-words encoders, so SDXL inherits their binding weakness. arXiv:2307.01952

### Cross-attention has a FIXED budget · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Cross-attention has a FIXED budget: every added token competes for the same attention mass, so non-visual words measurably starve the visual ones (attention dilution is real, not folklore).**

Zhang et al. (Attention Regulation) show cross-attention layers 'disproportionately focus on certain tokens', and that correct generations have attention EVENLY distributed across the relevant tokens while failures show a few tokens dominating and others 'neglected'. Because softmax attention sums to 1 across all prompt tokens, adding a backstory clause does not add a new channel — it redistributes a fixed pie. The narrative tokens, having no visual referent, still consume attention mass and pull it away from 'olive jacket' and 'red scar'. This is the literal mechanism of the studio's T5 failure: the grief-prose didn't just fail to help, it actively diluted the depictable tokens.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Treat the prompt as a zero-sum attention budget. Spend every token on a visible attribute. Cut filler ('a person who is', 'we can see that', 'the kind of'), connective backstory, and mood-prose — each one steals attention from a feature you actually want rendered. Shorter, denser, all-visual prompts render more faithfully than long narrative ones.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed and mechanistically sound — this is NOT folklore. Each row of the cross-attention map is softmax-normalized and sums to 1, so token attention is literally a fixed/zero-sum budget; published analysis shows per-token attention scales roughly as 1/(competing tokens) and that adding tokens progressively weakens the weight on any given token ('score dilution': near-tie distractors inflate the softmax denominator). Enhancing Semantic Fidelity / Attention Regulation (arXiv:2403.06381) confirms cross-attention 'disproportionately focuses on certain tokens,' that correct-semantics samples show attention 'more evenly distributed across relevant tokens,' and that token dominance/neglect degrades fidelity. The prompt_rule (spend tokens on visible attributes, cut filler) follows. One honest caveat: the dilution is statistical/uneven, not a strict guarantee that each added word subtracts equally — ungrounded words destabilize the distribution rather than cleanly 'starving' a fixed amount per token. The directional claim holds.
- **Sources:** [Enhancing Semantic Fidelity in Text-to-Image Synthesis: Attention Regulation in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06381) (2024) — Cross-attention disproportionately focuses on certain tokens; correct semantics correlate with attention evenly distributed across relevant tokens, while dominance/neglect of tokens degrades fidelity. arXiv:2403.06381 ; [Prompt Engineering for Stable Diffusion / 30kwps 'What is a Token'](https://portkey.ai/blog/prompt-engineering-for-stable-diffusion/) (2024) — Tokens compete for attention; a detail buried in a 48-token prompt gets less attention than the same detail as token 2-3 of a 20-token prompt.

### Describe what is VISIBLE, not what is TRUE' is forced by… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**'Describe what is VISIBLE, not what is TRUE' is forced by reporting bias in the training captions — the encoder literally never learned to depict inferred/contextual facts.**

Onoe-style reporting-bias work shows web captions (LAION etc.) follow Grice's maxim: humans omit the visually obvious and instead report the noteworthy/inferred ('parked at the beach', 'after the funeral') rather than 'a red car, four doors, chrome trim'. So the encoder's training signal systematically UNDER-represents plain visible attributes and contains almost no signal linking causal backstory to pixels. A token like 'the patch is faded because he stopped caring' has no learned visual consequence — the 'because he stopped caring' half is invisible to the model. The fix is not better phrasing of the intent; it is replacing intent with its visible RESULT.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Write the screenshot, not the script. For each canon fact, ask 'what would a frame-grab show?' Backstory ('faded because neglected') → visible result ('faded, frayed-edge cloth patch, loose thread'). Emotion ('worn by grief') → visible result ('red-rimmed eyes, three-day stubble, stained collar'). Never prompt causation, intent, history, or off-screen truth.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed. 'Scale Can't Overcome Pragmatics' (arXiv:2602.23351) directly supports it: captions describe the noteworthy/inferred not the visually obvious (Gricean reporting bias — its own example: people write 'at the game today!' not 'a photo of 37 people standing behind a field'), VLMs under-learn the suppressed skills (it names spatial reasoning, temporal reasoning, negation, counting), and 'scaling data size, model size, and to multiple languages does not result in emergence of these skills by default.' T5 grounding sub-claim also holds (Raffel et al. 2020: trained text-only on the C4 / Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, no image grounding). Minor precision note: reporting bias means visible-but-unremarkable attributes are UNDER-represented in captions, so the encoder learned them weakly — not that it 'literally never learned' them; the rhetorical 'never' overshoots slightly but the prompt_rule (write the screenshot, not the script) is correct.
- **Sources:** [Scale Can't Overcome Pragmatics: The Impact of Reporting Bias on Vision-Language Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23351) (2026) — Captions describe the noteworthy/inferred, not the visually obvious (Gricean reporting bias); VLMs therefore under-learn purely-visible attributes and cannot be fixed by scale alone. arXiv:2602.23351 ; [Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683) (Raffel et al., 2020) — T5 is trained purely on text (C4) with no image grounding, so in FLUX/Chroma its 'understanding' of a word is linguistic, not visual — it routes co-occurrence statistics, not depictions, to the diffusion model. arXiv:1910.10683

### ❌ DON'T — more descriptive words / richer emotional language = better… · `avoid` · community-claim

**FOLKLORE-DEBUNKED: 'more descriptive words / richer emotional language = better image' and 'keyword spam fills it in' are false for these encoders.**

The community habit of piling on evocative, emotional, and narrative adjectives ('hauntingly beautiful, deeply sorrowful, a soul worn thin') is counterproductive: per the attention-dilution and brittleness evidence, those tokens add ungrounded directions that steal attention from depictable ones and destabilize the embedding (the studio's exact failure). Equally, 'just keep adding keywords' fails because (a) CLIP truncates past 75 and (b) bag-of-words binding degrades as you add competing nouns. The real lever is depictable DENSITY (visible specifics per token), not word count or emotional intensity. Magic-keyword lists ('masterpiece, 8k, trending on artstation') are weak, dataset-specific aesthetic nudges, not semantic content — harmless filler at best, attention-thieves at worst.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]

- **For the pipeline:** Audit every prompt by deleting each word and asking 'does removing this change a pixel?' If no, cut it. Replace emotional/quality adjectives with the visible cause of that impression. Cap aesthetic-tag boilerplate to a few proven tokens at the very end where truncation can claim them harmlessly. Measure prompts by visible-attribute count, not length.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** anti-pattern
- **Verify:** UNVERIFIABLE
- **Sources:** [On the Brittleness of CLIP Text Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04247) (2025) — Abstract/non-visual words are encoded unreliably and certain tokens dominate the embedding — adding emotional/narrative words destabilizes rather than enriches the conditioning. arXiv:2511.04247 ; [Enhancing Semantic Fidelity (Attention Regulation in Diffusion Models)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06381) (2024) — Extra tokens redistribute a fixed attention budget; ungrounded words cause dominance/neglect imbalance that lowers fidelity, disproving 'more words = better'. arXiv:2403.06381

### LLM-based encoders (Qwen2.5-VL for Qwen-Image, Qwen3-4B for… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**LLM-based encoders (Qwen2.5-VL for Qwen-Image, Qwen3-4B for Z-Image) parse structure, negation and relations FAR better than CLIP — but they reward a different prompt SHAPE (detailed structured description, often via a system-prompt rewrite).**

Qwen-Image (Qwen2.5-VL) and Z-Image (Qwen3-4B) feed an actual LLM's hidden states as conditioning. Because Qwen2.5-VL is vision-language ALIGNED and Qwen3 is a strong instruction LM, these encoders retain syntax, count, spatial relations, and negation that CLIP destroys. Qwen-Image is explicitly trained/used with a system prompt that REWRITES the user prompt into a dense, detailed, structured description (the recommended 'magic prompt' path produces short-summary + medium-detail + object tags + long fine-grained caption). So the failure mode flips: terse tag-soup underperforms; rich, well-organized depictable description wins — and it tolerates structure CLIP can't. Still text/LLM, still no benefit from un-depictable intent: backstory remains inert.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** For Qwen-Image / Z-Image, write a structured, paragraph-style visual description (subject → appearance → clothing/material → pose → lighting → framing), and lean on the model's prompt-rewrite/system-prompt path rather than fighting it with SDXL-style comma tags. You may use clear spatial/relational/negation phrasing here ('standing to the left of the crate, no helmet') — these encoders handle it. Keep it all visible: structure is rewarded, mood-prose still is not.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen-VL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed on architecture. Qwen-Image (arXiv:2508.02324) uses Qwen2.5-VL as the text feature extractor (language/vision spaces pre-aligned, 'more suitable for T2I than language-based models'), with task-specific system prompts and recaptioning into four variants — short (<15 words) / medium / object-tags / long fine-grained — exactly as claimed. Z-Image (arXiv:2511.22699) uses the lightweight Qwen3-4B as text encoder for bilingual instruction alignment, concatenating text tokens with image/VAE tokens in a single-stream S3-DiT — an LLM encoder, not a CLIP contrastive one. These are decoder-LM/VLM encoders that handle structure/relations/negation far better than CLIP, and the structured-paragraph + system-prompt-rewrite prompt shape is the documented intended interface. Caveat: 'FAR better at negation/relations' is directionally correct (LLM encoders are not subject to CLIP's joint-embedding geometric ceiling) but is an architectural inference plus reporting-bias-paper support, not a head-to-head benchmark in these specific reports; treat as well-grounded but not numerically proven.
- **Sources:** [Qwen-Image Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02324) (2025) — Qwen-Image uses Qwen2.5-VL as the text feature extractor (language/vision spaces pre-aligned) with task-specific system prompts that guide detail-rich T2I descriptions; recaptioning produces short/medium/tag/long fine-grained variants. arXiv:2508.02324 ; [Z-Image: Efficient Image Generation Foundation Model (S3-DiT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22699) (2025) — Z-Image uses Qwen3-4B as the text encoder for bilingual instruction alignment, concatenating text tokens with image tokens in a single-stream DiT — an LLM encoder, not a CLIP-style contrastive one. arXiv:2511.22699

### T5-XXL (FLUX/Chroma) gives token-level structure and… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**T5-XXL (FLUX/Chroma) gives token-level structure and handles long depictable descriptions — but it is text-only, so it still cannot ground abstract intent; longer just means more room for visible detail, not for backstory.**

In FLUX, CLIP-L supplies only a single pooled global vector (scale/shift modulation) while T5-XXL supplies the fine-grained per-token features the U-Net actually cross-attends to. T5 keeps word order and clause structure (unlike bag-of-words CLIP), so it binds attributes and follows compositional phrasing far better — this is why FLUX rewards natural-language, comma-light, descriptive prose. BUT T5 is trained on pure text (Raffel 2020): it knows 'grief co-occurs with crying' linguistically, yet has zero pixel grounding, so it routes that as a vague statistical nudge, not a depiction. The studio's mushy result is exactly this: T5 happily encoded the grief-prose into a real-valued direction with no visual target, diluting the depictable tokens it was concatenated with.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** For FLUX/Chroma, write fluent descriptive sentences but fill them ONLY with visible specifics: 'A weathered man in a faded olive jacket with a frayed cloth patch on the left shoulder; deep under-eye shadows, three-day stubble, jaw set, gaze lowered.' Use the longer budget to add MORE visible attributes (lighting, material, framing, pose), never to add mood/history. Put the most load-bearing visual subject early.
- **Engine:** T5 · **Base:** T5 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed. FLUX architecture: CLIP-L enters only as a pooled global embedding for scale/shift modulation (the 'vec'/vector_in path), while T5-XXL supplies fine-grained token-level features to cross-attention (DeepWiki FLUX architecture; corroborated by 'Demystifying Flux Architecture' arXiv:2507.09595, which states Flux's text branch is T5-XXL-driven with CLIP as pooled modulation only). T5 is text-only (C4, no image grounding — Raffel et al.), so it routes linguistic co-occurrence, not depictions. The 'longer = more room for visible detail, not backstory' guidance is consistent with the reporting-bias + attention-dilution findings above. Token budget for FLUX confirmed under finding 7 (dev 512 / schnell 256).
- **Sources:** [FLUX Model Architecture (DeepWiki) — CLIP pooled vs T5 token features](https://deepwiki.com/black-forest-labs/flux/4.1-flux-model-architecture) (2024) — FLUX uses CLIP-L only as a pooled global embedding for scale/shift modulation; T5-XXL provides the fine-grained token-level features fed to the cross-attention stream. ; [Demystifying Flux Architecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09595) (2025) — Flux's text branch is driven by T5-XXL token embeddings; CLIP features enter only as pooled modulation, so prompt semantics are carried by T5. arXiv:2507.09595

### There is a PROVEN geometric ceiling · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**There is a PROVEN geometric ceiling: no CLIP-style joint embedding can simultaneously do basic description + attribute binding + spatial relations + negation.**

Multiple 2025-26 results (the 'Is CLIP ideal?' line and negation-geometry work) establish that CLIP's single shared embedding space mathematically cannot represent more than ~two of {object identity, attribute binding, spatial relations, negation} at once; negated/affirmative queries collapse to near-identical embeddings. So 'NOT wearing a hat', 'behind the barrel', 'a cube behind a sphere' are encoder-level impossible for CLIP — they are not prompt-skill problems. T5/Qwen LLM encoders handle these far better because they retain syntactic structure, but on SDXL you are hard-capped.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL/CLIP: never rely on negation (no 'without', 'no', 'not') — express the positive visible state instead ('bare head', 'closed door'). Don't trust spatial relations in a single CLIP prompt; compose them with layout tools/inpainting/control. Reserve negation and spatial logic for the T5/Qwen pipelines, and even there keep them simple.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CORRECTED: The cited result is REAL but the finding UNDERSTATES it. 'Is CLIP ideal? No. Can we fix it? Yes!' (arXiv:2503.08723) proves that 'no CLIP-like joint embedding space exists which can correctly do any TWO of the following at the same time: 1. basic descriptions/image content, 2. attribute binding, 3. spatial location and relationships, 4. negation.' So the true ceiling is that you cannot reliably do even TWO of the four simultaneously — strictly stronger than the finding's 'cannot do more than two (i.e., at most two are OK).' Correct the framing from 'at most two simultaneously' to 'cannot reliably do even two of the four at once.' Practical prompt_rule (don't lean on negation or spatial relations in a single CLIP prompt; express positive visible states; compose spatial layout with control tools) is correct and if anything more justified than the finding implies. Negation sub-claim corroborated by arXiv:2603.20554: a negation direction exists in CLIP space (geometric, not lexical), manipulable by representation engineering — note this paper frames negation as a recoverable geometric direction rather than asserting affirmative/negated embeddings are flatly indistinguishable, so soften that secondary phrasing.
- **Sources:** [Is CLIP ideal? No. Can we fix it? Yes!](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08723) (2025) — No CLIP-like joint embedding can correctly do more than two of: basic description, attribute binding, spatial relations, negation — a structural impossibility. arXiv:2503.08723 ; [When Negation Is a Geometry Problem in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20554) (2026) — Joint-embedding VLMs collapse affirmative and negated queries into near-indistinguishable embeddings; negation is a geometric, not lexical, failure. arXiv:2603.20554

### Token limits are HARD and truncation is SILENT · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Token limits are HARD and truncation is SILENT — work past them and the tail of your prompt (often the most specific details, placed last) is simply discarded.**

CLIP-L and OpenCLIP-bigG: 77 tokens including BOS/EOS (≈75 usable), ≈300-375 chars at ~4-5 chars/token; diffusers truncates and warns, but in many UIs the warning is unseen. ComfyUI/A1111 don't truncate — they CHUNK into 75-token blocks, encode each separately, and concatenate, so cross-block attribute binding is lost (a detail in chunk 2 cannot bind to a subject in chunk 1); 'BREAK' forces a chunk boundary. T5-XXL: 512 tokens on FLUX.1-dev/Chroma, but only 256 on FLUX.1-schnell, and you must pass max_sequence_length=512 or it silently caps lower. Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image): effectively no practical prompt cap (32k context, YaRN-extendable). Qwen3-4B (Z-Image): large LLM context, no 77-style cap. The danger: writers front-load mood-prose and the truncator eats the depictable specifics at the end.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Budget consciously per target. SDXL: keep the whole prompt under ~75 tokens (~300 chars) and put load-bearing visible attributes FIRST so nothing critical is in the truncated tail; avoid relying on BREAK-split details binding across chunks. FLUX-dev/Chroma: stay under 512 tokens and explicitly set max_sequence_length=512; on schnell assume a 256-token wall. Qwen/Z-Image: length is not the constraint — depictability and structure are.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Token numbers verified exactly: CLIP context = 77 tokens, with diffusers truncating longer prompts (HF diffusers issue #2136 confirms the 77-token wall; the documented warning is 'because CLIP can only handle sequences up to 77 tokens'). FLUX T5-XXL = up to 512 tokens on dev, 256 on schnell; using the full 512 requires passing max_sequence_length=512 (FLUX.1-dev discussion #43). Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) context is up to 32,768 tokens (YaRN beyond that), so for Qwen/Z-Image length is genuinely not the binding constraint — depictability/structure is, as the finding states. Two honesty caveats on 'silent': (1) diffusers DOES emit a truncation warning for CLIP, so it is loud in logs even if silent in output; (2) SDXL's effective per-encoder limit is 77 tokens each, and the popular '~75 usable' figure comes from the BOS/EOS overhead (75 content + 2 special). The practical rule (front-load load-bearing visible attributes, don't bury critical details in the truncated tail) is correct.
- **Sources:** [HuggingFace diffusers — CLIP 77-token limit & truncation warning](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/2136) (2023) — CLIP context length is 77 tokens; diffusers truncates longer prompts and emits a 'truncated because CLIP can only handle sequences up to 77 tokens' warning. ; [FLUX.1-dev discussion — T5 512 (256 on schnell), max_sequence_length](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev/discussions/43) (2024) — FLUX T5-XXL handles up to 512 tokens (256 on schnell); CLIP stays at 77; full 512 requires explicitly passing max_sequence_length=512.

## Structured / compositional prompting

### BREAK and 75-token chunking are CLIP-ONLY plumbing · `recommended` · community-claim

**BREAK and 75-token chunking are CLIP-ONLY plumbing — concatenated chunks don't cross-attend, so split by semantic group, not mid-phrase.**

A1111/ComfyUI handle >75-token CLIP prompts by cutting into 75-token chunks, padding each with BOS/EOS, encoding independently, and concatenating along the sequence axis. Tokens in different chunks never attend to each other and weights don't cross the boundary. BREAK forces the cut where you want it (pads the current chunk, starts fresh). FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image have NO chunking — BREAK is meaningless text to them.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL only: if you must exceed 75 tokens, insert BREAK at semantic seams (e.g. after the full character block, before the environment block) so related attributes stay in one chunk and don't get severed mid-phrase. Do not rely on chunk 2+ for critical attributes — cross-chunk binding is weak. On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image: never type BREAK; just write a tight prompt under the cap.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. comfyui-clip-with-break (dfl) splits the prompt at the BREAK keyword (regex \s*\bBREAK\b\s*), encodes each segment SEPARATELY through CLIP, then concatenates the conditioning. Because each chunk is encoded independently before concat, there is no cross-chunk self-attention — so attributes severed across a BREAK don't bind, confirming 'split by semantic seam, not mid-phrase' and 'don't rely on chunk 2+ for critical attributes.' This is CLIP plumbing (it exists to work around CLIP's 75-token-per-chunk limit; SDXL dual-encoder support just applies the same trick to both CLIP encoders). T5/Qwen/Z-Image have a single long context window and no chunking, so typing BREAK there is meaningless — correct. The only thing the cited source doesn't literally spell out is the words 'don't cross-attend,' but independent-encode-then-concat necessarily implies no cross-chunk attention, so the inference is sound.
- **Sources:** [dfl/comfyui-clip-with-break (DeepWiki)](https://deepwiki.com/dfl/comfyui-clip-with-break) (dfl, 2024) — Prompts are split into 75-token chunks by the BREAK keyword and concatenated into a single conditioning; each chunk is encoded independently. ; [Stable Diffusion prompt syntax: BREAK and chunking](https://www.generativelabs.com/insights/prompt-syntax-for-stable-diffusion-faq) (Generative Labs, 2024) — BREAK ends a chunk early, pads with empty tokens, and starts the next chunk fresh; weights and attention do not cross chunk boundaries.

### CLIP's effective attention span is ~20 tokens, not 77 · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CLIP's effective attention span is ~20 tokens, not 77 — front-load the subject and key visual attributes.**

CLIP was trained on short web captions, so position embeddings beyond ~20 tokens are under-trained; empirically CLIP's effective length is ~20 tokens and self-attention is biased toward early tokens. The 77-token cap is a hard ceiling, but tokens 21-75 carry weak, degraded signal even when not truncated. This is the single most important structural fact for SDXL prompting.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL (and the CLIP-L side of FLUX), put the subject + 3-5 highest-priority visual attributes in the FIRST ~20 tokens (~75-90 chars). Everything after token ~20 is decoration with diminishing returns. Lead with 'weary female knight, faded green tabard, short silver hair' — never bury the subject behind quality words or mood.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. Long-CLIP (Zhang et al., 2024, arXiv:2403.15378) states verbatim in its abstract: 'The length of the text token is restricted to 77, and an empirical study shows the actual effective length is even less than 20.' Exact numbers: hard cap = 77 tokens (75 content + BOS + EOS); effective length < 20 tokens. Mechanism (under-trained position embeddings past ~20) is the paper's motivation for its position-embedding stretching, even if not quoted as a single sentence. The front-loading prompt_rule follows directly. The '~75-90 chars' rough equivalence for 20 tokens is a reasonable heuristic (≈4 chars/token) but is the verifier's own approximation, not a paper figure — treat the char count as soft.
- **Sources:** [Long-CLIP: Unlocking the Long-Text Capability of CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15378) (Zhang, Wei, Wu, et al., 2024) — CLIP's effective text length is merely ~20 tokens because position embeddings past token 20 are inadequately trained; only the first 20 positions are well-trained. arXiv:2403.15378 ; [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (Radford, Kim, Hallacy, et al., 2021) — CLIP's text encoder uses a fixed 76-token context (77 with BOS/EOS) and was trained predominantly on short image-alt-text captions. arXiv:2103.00020

### Encoder type dictates token-ORDER sensitivity · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Encoder type dictates token-ORDER sensitivity: CLIP is strongly order/position sensitive (front-load); T5 and LLM encoders are bidirectional/context-aware (write coherent sentences, bind attributes explicitly).**

CLIP has learned absolute position embeddings and an early-token attention bias, so order matters a lot — first tokens dominate. T5 uses bidirectional full-visibility attention (every token attends to every other), making it far less order-sensitive and good at attribute binding through grammar. Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3 are causal LLMs that read the prompt as instruction-following language with a prepended system prompt — they reward clear, well-structured natural language and explicit spatial/relational phrasing over keyword soup.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Match structure to encoder. CLIP/SDXL: comma-separated, subject-first, highest priority earliest. T5/FLUX/Chroma: full grammatical sentences with explicit attribute binding ('the knight's tabard is faded green' so 'faded green' binds to 'tabard', not the sky) and explicit spatial language ('centered, three-quarter view'). Qwen-Image/Z-Image (LLM): natural descriptive paragraphs, optionally LLM-expanded; spell out layout, materials, and any rendered text verbatim in quotes. Don't paste the SAME prompt across encoder families.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. SDXL (Podell et al. 2023, arXiv:2307.01952) concatenates penultimate-layer features of CLIP ViT-L + OpenCLIP ViT-bigG and adds bigG's POOLED text embedding as conditioning — two CLIP encoders with absolute (learned) position embeddings, hence order/front-loading sensitivity (consistent with finding 0). HF T5 docs confirm the T5 encoder uses fully-visible (bidirectional) self-attention — every token attends to all others — so it is far less token-order-sensitive than a causal model, supporting 'write coherent sentences, bind attributes explicitly.' The structural prescriptions (CLIP: comma tags subject-first; T5: grammatical sentences with explicit attribute binding + explicit spatial language; LLM Qwen/Z-Image: natural paragraphs, quote rendered text verbatim) are sound and consistent with each model's training. Caveat: 'bidirectional ⇒ order-INSENSITIVE' is a matter of degree, not absolute — bidirectional attention reduces but does not eliminate order effects (word order still changes meaning and binding). 'Explicit binding matters more than raw position' is the accurate takeaway, which the rule captures. 'Don't paste the same prompt across encoder families' is correct and the load-bearing instruction.
- **Sources:** [SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01952) (Podell, English, Lacey, Blattmann, Dockhorn, Müller, Penna, Rombach, 2023) — SDXL concatenates the penultimate token features of CLIP-L and OpenCLIP-bigG and adds bigG's pooled text embedding as conditioning — two CLIP encoders with absolute position embeddings. arXiv:2307.01952 ; [T5 documentation — bidirectional encoder](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/t5) (Hugging Face / Raffel et al., 2020) — T5's encoder uses fully-visible (bidirectional) self-attention so every token attends to all others, making it far less token-order-sensitive than a causal model.

### Hard token limits differ wildly per encoder and ALL… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Hard token limits differ wildly per encoder and ALL truncate the tail SILENTLY — schnell at 256 is the trap.**

Caps: CLIP 77 (75 usable), FLUX-dev T5 512, FLUX-schnell T5 256, Chroma T5 ~512, Qwen-Image 1024 default, Z-Image 512 (1024 local). None raise an error — the tail past the cap is dropped silently. FLUX-schnell's 256-token cap is half of dev's and bites mid-prompt on character sheets; a long description can lose its back half before encoding.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Pin a per-encoder character budget and order prompts so the most important content is always before the cap: CLIP first ~75 chars critical / ~300 hard; schnell ~1000 chars; dev/Chroma/Z-Image ~2000 chars; Qwen-Image ~3000+ chars. Put a token counter in the pipeline; never assume a prompt 'fit.' Verify Qwen-Image runs at max_sequence_length=1024 (diffusers bug #12075 caused RoPE artifacts from wrong padding).

FLUX T5-XXL = 512 tokens on FLUX.1-dev, 256 on FLUX.1-schnell (HF discussion #43; also the diffusers FLUX docs note the guidance-distilled dev variant has effectively no max_sequence_length ceiling enforced the same way). Qwen-Image default max_sequence_length = 1024 and MUST stay padded to 1024 (diffusers #12075 — padding to batch-longest caused RoPE artifacts: 'minecraft' produced shape [1,5,3584] instead of [1,1024,3584]). So 'all truncate silently' is folklore-flavored overstatement; the safe takeaway (pin a per-encoder budget + add a token counter) is correct. The verifier's specific char budgets (~75/1000/2000/3000 chars) are rough heuristics, not spec'd limits — treat as soft guidance, count TOKENS not chars.
- **Sources:** [FLUX.1-dev: Input tokens limited (BFL HF discussion)](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev/discussions/43) (Black Forest Labs / community, 2024) — FLUX T5-XXL handles up to 512 tokens (256 on schnell); the CLIP encoder is fixed at 77; prompts exceeding the limit are truncated. ; [Qwen Image prompt encoding is not padding to max seq len (diffusers #12075)](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/12075) (huggingface/diffusers contributors, 2025) — Qwen-Image default max_sequence_length is 1024 and must remain padded to 1024; padding to the batch-longest length instead caused RoPE position-embedding artifacts.

### ❌ DON'T — masterpiece / best quality / very aesthetic' work ONLY on… · `avoid` · community-claim

**'masterpiece / best quality / very aesthetic' work ONLY on Danbooru-trained anime bases — on base SDXL/FLUX/Qwen they are folklore filler.**

Anime fine-tunes (Pony, Animagine, Illustrious, NoobAI) were trained with explicit quality-tier tags ('masterpiece', 'best quality', score_9) as learned conditioning, so those tokens genuinely shift output quality on THOSE models. Base SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, and Z-Image never saw that vocabulary as a quality signal — the words are just generic tokens that consume budget (and on CLIP, burn precious early-token positions). Carrying them onto a photoreal/JRPG-painterly base is cargo-cult.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]

- **For the pipeline:** Use quality tags ('masterpiece', 'best quality', 'score_9') ONLY when the checkpoint is a Danbooru/booru-tag anime fine-tune that documents them. On base SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, Z-Image: drop them and instead name concrete style descriptors the model actually learned ('hand-painted 2.5D JRPG key art, soft rim light, gouache texture'). Never spend CLIP's first 20 tokens on 'masterpiece, best quality.'
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** anti-pattern
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded enough to confirm, with the folklore-DEBUNKED grounding being the correct label. Illustrious (Onoma AI, arXiv:2409.19946) and the booru-tagging guide establish that quality tiers (masterpiece/best quality, and the Pony 'score_9' family) are learned tokens from Danbooru/booru community-rating buckets baked into anime fine-tunes (Pony, Animagine, Illustrious) — that is WHY they condition output on those bases. The Tech Tactician guide explicitly notes base SDXL was trained 'with a heavier emphasis on Natural Language captions,' which is the mechanism for why booru quality tags don't reliably fire on base SDXL/FLUX/Qwen. So 'masterpiece, best quality' on a base/natural-language model is unsupported filler that also burns CLIP's scarce first-20 tokens (ties to finding 0). Use concrete learned style descriptors instead — correct. The one nuance the sources don't let us assert is a hard 'zero effect on base SDXL' — the tokens still exist in CLIP's vocab and may nudge weakly; the right claim is 'not the reliable quality lever they are on booru fine-tunes,' which is what the rule says.
- **Sources:** [Booru-Style Tagging, and How To Use It With SDXL Anime Model Prompts](https://techtactician.com/booru-style-tagging-sdxl-anime-prompts-guide/) (Tech Tactician, 2026) — Quality meta-tags like masterpiece/best quality are effective specifically because anime fine-tunes (Pony, Animagine, Illustrious) were heavily trained on Danbooru datasets that used those tags. ; [Illustrious: an Open Advanced Illustration Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19946) (Onoma AI Research, 2024) — Illustrious and related models are trained on Danbooru tag vocabularies including quality tiers, which is why booru/quality tags condition output on these specific bases. arXiv:2409.19946

### Negative prompts are a CFG mechanic, not a 'forbidden… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Negative prompts are a CFG mechanic, not a 'forbidden words' list — and they DON'T exist on guidance-distilled models (FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo).**

CFG runs the model twice — a conditioned (positive) pass and an unconditioned pass — and pushes the result away from the unconditioned prediction: eps = eps(neg) + scale*(eps(pos) - eps(neg)). A negative prompt simply REPLACES the empty unconditioned branch with a second real encode, steering away from it. This requires two passes. FLUX-dev/schnell use *guidance distillation* (guidance baked into a single pass) so they have no genuine unconditioned branch and ignore negative prompts. Z-Image-Turbo is distilled and uses NO CFG at all. Chroma is de-distilled and RE-ENABLES true CFG, so its negative prompt is real (and uses the same T5 cap).  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Maintain negative prompts ONLY for SDXL and Chroma (true-CFG models). For FLUX-dev/schnell and Z-Image-Turbo, delete the negative prompt entirely — it does nothing; bake exclusions into the positive prompt instead ('clean background' rather than negative 'cluttered'). On SDXL, keep negatives a short tag list of genuine failure modes (extra fingers, lowres, jpeg artifacts), not a wishlist — every neg token is a real second encode that steers the unconditioned branch.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CORRECTED: Mechanism CONFIRMED, but the absolute 'they DON'T exist on FLUX-dev' needs one correction. CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022, arXiv:2207.12598) interpolates conditioned vs unconditioned predictions; negative prompting swaps the unconditioned branch for an unwanted-feature-conditioned one — correct framing. Z-Image-Turbo's own card confirms it is a few-step distilled model that 'does not rely on classifier-free guidance during inference… does not use negative prompts at all' — so for Z-Image-Turbo and FLUX-schnell, dropping the negative is right. CORRECTION for FLUX-DEV: FLUX-dev ships GUIDANCE-distilled (a guidance_embeds scalar baked in, not a CFG term), so the standard negative_prompt is a no-op AT guidance_scale's normal path — BUT diffusers exposes true_cfg_scale (>1) which re-enables a genuine unconditioned/negative branch on FLUX-dev (the FLUX docs use true_cfg_scale=4.0; community confirms 'true CFG' restores negative prompts at ~2x compute). So 'delete the negative prompt entirely — it does nothing' is right by DEFAULT but wrong as an absolute: a negative prompt DOES work on FLUX-dev when true_cfg_scale>1. Schnell (timestep-distilled, guidance_scale must be 0) genuinely has no negative path. The SDXL/Chroma true-CFG distinction and 'short tag list of real failure modes, not a wishlist' advice are sound.
- **Sources:** [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Ho, Salimans, 2022) — CFG interpolates between conditioned and unconditioned model predictions; negative prompting replaces the unconditioned branch with a prediction conditioned on the unwanted features. arXiv:2207.12598 ; [Questions about guidance_embeds and guidance_scale in flux-dev and flux-schnell (BFL #63)](https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux/issues/63) (Black Forest Labs / community, 2024) — FLUX-dev uses distilled (embedded) guidance and schnell uses none, so traditional CFG and negative prompts do not apply the way they do on SDXL.

### Prompt weighting (word:1.3) is a CLIP/embedding-scaling trick · `recommended` · community-claim

**Prompt weighting (word:1.3) is a CLIP/embedding-scaling trick — it does NOT transfer to T5 or LLM encoders.**

Weighting in A1111/ComfyUI/compel works by scaling the CLIP token embedding vectors before they reach the U-Net (compel interpolates toward/away from the empty-prompt embedding; ComfyUI applies a literal multiplier on the embedding). There is no equivalent learned hook in T5 or in LLM encoders (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3) — typing '(word:1.3)' into a FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image prompt just inserts literal parenthesis-and-number TOKENS that the encoder reads as text, usually degrading the result. Also note A1111 normalizes weights while ComfyUI uses a raw multiplier, so the same syntax differs across UIs.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Use (term:1.1-1.3) weighting ONLY on SDXL/CLIP. On T5 (FLUX/Chroma) and LLM encoders (Qwen-Image, Z-Image), emphasize via NATURAL LANGUAGE instead: repeat or foreground the concept, use stronger adjectives, or restructure the sentence ('the central focus is X'). Strip all weighting parentheses out of FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image prompts. Keep SDXL weights gentle (<=1.3); high weights fry the embedding.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. compel (Damian Stewart) implements weighting as a CLIP-token-embedding operation (re-weighting the embedding tensor, with downweighting via attention-masking toward the empty/removed-token state) and is built/tested against CLIP-conditioned StableDiffusionPipelines; it does not define a T5 weighting semantics. The (word:1.3) multiplier is a per-chunk CLIP-embedding scale (ComfyUI literal multiplier vs A1111 normalized). On T5/LLM encoders there is no equivalent embedding-blend hook, so parenthetical weights are at best ignored and at worst injected as literal characters. Emphasize via natural language instead — correct. Minor nuance: some FLUX ComfyUI nodes parse weighting syntax and apply it to the CLIP-L branch only (not T5), so 'strip parens out of FLUX prompts' is the safe default; weights there would only ever touch the CLIP-L side, never T5. Keep SDXL weights gentle (≤1.3) is sound craft advice (no single citation, but consistent with embedding-blend mechanics).
- **Sources:** [Stable Diffusion prompt syntax: parentheses, brackets, weights, and BREAK](https://www.generativelabs.com/insights/prompt-syntax-for-stable-diffusion-faq) (Generative Labs, 2024) — Weighting and BREAK operate on CLIP-chunk embeddings; ComfyUI treats (word:1.5) as a literal multiplier while A1111 normalizes, and weights do not cross chunk boundaries. ; [compel — prompt weighting library](https://github.com/damian0815/compel) (Damian Stewart, 2023) — compel implements weighting by blending CLIP token embeddings toward/away from the empty-string embedding — an embedding-space operation specific to CLIP-conditioned models.

### T5-based diffusion models (FLUX, Chroma) do NOT respond to… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**T5-based diffusion models (FLUX, Chroma) do NOT respond to non-depictable / narrative tokens — prose like 'worn by grief' is dead weight that dilutes the visual tokens.**

Although T5 was trained on the C4 natural-language corpus full of abstract text, diffusion models conditioned on T5 simply do not act on non-visual prompts — the visual-relevant subspace of T5's embedding is small and the rest is redundant for image synthesis. Abstract/backstory tokens still consume the token budget and shift the mean of the conditioning, pulling the image toward a generic average. This is the direct mechanism behind the studio's 'mushy generic' failure.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** For T5 encoders, write ONLY depictable facts. Convert every emotional/backstory clause into its visual consequence: NOT 'worn by grief, guarded and steady' but 'hollow cheeks, dark under-eye shadows, jaw set, eyes narrowed, shoulders squared.' NOT 'a patch faded because of a long war' but 'sun-bleached frayed shoulder patch, threadbare edges.' If a token can't be drawn, delete it.
- **Engine:** T5 · **Base:** T5 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. 'Scaling Down Text Encoders of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models' (Wang et al., CVPR 2025) states that because T5 was trained on the C4 corpus containing significant non-visual data, 'diffusion models with T5 encoder do not respond to those non-visual prompts, indicating redundancy in representational power.' Concrete evidence in their Fig. 2: a non-visual prompt ('Love is patient') yields a near-floor CLIP score of 13.68 (image fails to align). The 'convert emotion to visual consequence / delete non-depictable tokens' rule is a sound operationalization. One scoping caveat: the paper's claim is about non-VISUAL prompts failing to condition the image, which supports the rule; it does not separately measure 'dilution' of co-present visual tokens, so the 'dilutes the visual tokens' phrasing is a reasonable but slightly stronger inference than the paper directly tests.
- **Sources:** [Scaling Down Text Encoders of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models](https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2025/papers/Wang_Scaling_Down_Text_Encoders_of_Text-to-Image_Diffusion_Models_CVPR_2025_paper.pdf) (Wang, et al., 2025) — Diffusion models with a T5 encoder do not respond to non-visual prompts; if a non-visual prompt is used the image does not align with it, indicating large redundancy in T5's representational power for image synthesis. ; [Exploring the Text-to-Image Latent Space (T5/Raffel)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683) (Raffel, Shazeer, Roberts, et al., 2020) — T5 is a general text-to-text transformer trained on the C4 web corpus (mostly non-visual language), establishing why much of its embedding capacity is irrelevant to image content. arXiv:1910.10683

### There is a length sweet spot, and it is encoder-specific · `recommended` · community-claim

**There is a length sweet spot, and it is encoder-specific — short for CLIP, medium-detailed for T5, long for LLM encoders; past the sweet spot you get dilution, not detail.**

Adding tokens raises the risk that the mean of the conditioning drifts toward generic and that attributes cross-bind. For CLIP the sweet spot is tiny (~20 effective tokens, community consensus 25-35 anime tags max before confusion). For T5/FLUX, mid-length explicit sentences win; piling on prose dilutes (the studio failure). For Qwen-Image/Z-Image, the official guidance is genuinely long detailed natural-language prompts — these LLM encoders are the ONE place where verbosity helps, because the model parses structure rather than averaging tokens.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Calibrate length to the encoder, don't max it out. SDXL: aim ~25-40 tokens of pure visual content, never pad to 75. FLUX/Chroma: 1-4 tight sentences of depictable facts (well under 256/512). Qwen-Image/Z-Image: write a full detailed paragraph (these reward it) — and ONLY here consider LLM-expanding a short prompt. If a JRPG character result is 'mushy/generic,' the fix is usually FEWER, more concrete tokens, not more.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded directionally. The CLIP-end is well-supported: Long-CLIP's <20-token effective length means text past ~20 tokens contributes under-trained position signal rather than usable detail — establishing a genuinely SHORT CLIP sweet spot, so 'aim ~25-40 visual tokens, never pad to 75' is sound (the exact 25-40 is a reasonable heuristic, not a measured optimum). The LLM-end is supported: Z-Image-Turbo's card says it 'works best with long and detailed prompts' (optionally LLM-enhanced) — confirming the long-reward end. The T5 'medium' middle is the least independently quantified point — there's no cited measurement of a FLUX dilution curve, so '1-4 tight sentences, well under 256/512' is craft heuristic consistent with finding 1 (depictable-only) rather than a benchmarked sweet spot. Net: the SHAPE of the claim (short/medium/long by encoder, with dilution past the sweet spot) is confirmed at both endpoints and reasonable in the middle; treat the specific token counts as guidance, not spec. 'If JRPG output is mushy, the fix is usually FEWER concrete tokens, not more' is the correct corollary of the CLIP finding.
- **Sources:** [Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo — Prompting Guide](https://huggingface.co/Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo/discussions/8) (Tongyi MAI (Alibaba), 2025) — Z-Image-Turbo works best with long, detailed natural-language prompts (optionally LLM-enhanced); it does not use CFG and has no negative-prompt path. ; [Long-CLIP: Unlocking the Long-Text Capability of CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15378) (Zhang, Wei, Wu, et al., 2024) — Because CLIP's effective length is ~20 tokens, adding text past that point yields under-trained position signal rather than usable detail — establishing a short CLIP sweet spot. arXiv:2403.15378

## Face / identity

### CLIP's effective attention dies around token ~20, not token 77 · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CLIP's effective attention dies around token ~20, not token 77 — late tokens are near-invisible even before truncation.**

Long-CLIP shows CLIP's absolute positional embeddings beyond ~position 20 are undertrained (training captions were short), so retrieval/conditioning strength flatlines after ~20 tokens. The 77-token cap is a hard ceiling, but the SOFT ceiling is ~20. In SDXL this hits both CLIP-L and bigG, and bigG's pooled-embedding global-gist path is dominated by the earliest high-salience tokens. A face descriptor buried at token 40 of an SDXL prompt is effectively whispered.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL, front-load face/identity descriptors into the FIRST ~10-15 tokens: e.g. 'sharp detailed face, [hair/eye/age], <character>, full-body, ...' NOT '...wandering a ruined keep at dusk, full-body, worn cloak, ... detailed face'. If you need a long SDXL prompt, use BREAK to start a fresh 75-token chunk so the face descriptor sits early in its own chunk.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed. Long-CLIP (arXiv:2403.15378) states 'the actual effective length for CLIP is merely 20 tokens' because positional embeddings for higher positions are inadequately trained (CLIP was trained on short captions); retrieval performance shows only slow growth past ~20 tokens. EXACT TOKEN FACTS: CLIP context = 77 tokens total = 76 usable after [SOS]/[EOS] bracketing (NOT 75 — the '75-token chunk' figure in the rule is the common A1111/ComfyUI convention that reserves SOS+EOS, i.e. 77-2=75 content tokens per chunk; both 75 and 76 appear depending on whether one EOS or SOS+EOS is counted). Absolute positional embeddings, BPE vocab ~49,408. The ~20-token effective window is a CLIP-specific finding and does NOT transfer to T5 (longer effective window) — the rule correctly scopes the BREAK/front-loading advice to SDXL/CLIP. Practical 'first 10-15 tokens' is heuristic, directionally correct, not a sourced exact number.
- **Sources:** [Long-CLIP: Unlocking the Long-Text Capability of CLIP](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.15378v1) (Zhang, Wu, et al., 2024) — CLIP's true effective length is ~20 tokens because positional embeddings for higher positions are inadequately trained; performance growth flattens once input exceeds ~20 tokens. arXiv:2403.15378 ; [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (Radford et al., 2021) — CLIP's text encoder uses a 77-token context with [SOS]/[EOS] bracketing and absolute positional embeddings, trained on short captions — the architectural source of the 77 cap and the short effective length. arXiv:2103.00020

### A face starves below a hard pixel floor · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**A face starves below a hard pixel floor: the VAE 8x downsample destroys facial detail BEFORE diffusion runs, so a 70px face in a full-body frame is already mush at the latent stage.**

Every SD/SDXL/FLUX/Qwen VAE compresses the image 8x per spatial dimension (e.g. 1024px -> 128x128 latent; 512px -> 64x64). A face occupying ~70px of a 1024px-tall full-body shot lands on roughly an 8x9 patch of latent — fewer cells than the face has features. Detail smaller than the 8px-per-cell threshold is gone before the first denoising step; no prompt token can recover information the VAE already discarded. This is an encoder-independent, upstream-of-text bottleneck.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** For a hero whose FACE matters, do not ask one full-body generation to carry it. Either (a) frame to portrait/cowboy-shot so the head occupies >=512px of frame, or (b) generate full-body first, then crop the head region and regenerate/upscale it as its own >=768px pass (inpaint or detailer), then composite. Treat 'face area in pixels' as a budget you spend, not a prompt you write.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Mechanism confirmed by official HF Diffusion Course: the SD VAE produces a 4-channel latent with a spatial reduction factor of 8, so a 512px image becomes a 4x64x64 latent. A 70px face occupies only ~8-9 latent pixels (70/8), so it is genuinely below the spatial resolution diffusion operates on. Nuance/correction: the official doc states the 8x reduction and 64x64 latent but does NOT itself state 'detail below the 8px grid is lost' as a sharp cliff — that framing is community inference (Efrat Taig Medium, strong-community), not an official claim. The reduction factor is exact and load-bearing; the 'hard floor / starves' phrasing is a reasonable but informal gloss on a soft compression, not a documented threshold. The prompt rule (frame to portrait so head >=512px, or generate + crop + detailer pass >=768px) is sound and matches established community face-fix practice. Note >=512px / >=768px are heuristic targets, not from the cited sources.
- **Sources:** [Unit 3: Stable Diffusion (HF Diffusion Course) — VAE 8x reduction factor](https://huggingface.co/learn/diffusion-course/en/unit3/1) (Hugging Face, 2023) — The SD VAE produces a 4-channel latent with a spatial reduction factor of 8, so a 512px image becomes a 64x64 latent — detail below the 8px grid is lost before diffusion. ; [VAE: The Latent Bottleneck — Why Image Generation Loses Fine Details](https://medium.com/@efrat_taig/vae-the-latent-bottleneck-why-image-generation-processes-lose-fine-details-a056dcd6015e) (Efrat Taig, 2024) — Small features such as faces and text are compressed in latent space and become blurry/distorted; many failures blamed on the diffusion model actually originate in VAE compression.

### ❌ DON'T — piling on quality tokens ('masterpiece, ultra-detailed… · `avoid` · community-claim

**FOLKLORE, DEBUNKED: piling on quality tokens ('masterpiece, ultra-detailed face, 8k, sharp facial features, perfect face, highly detailed') does NOT add face pixels — and on CLIP it can crowd the face descriptor past the ~20-token effective window.**

'Detailed face' / 'portrait' style tokens are real and mildly helpful — community testing shows 'detailed face' nudges rendering quality — but they operate on the diffusion prior's notion of 'a nice face,' not on the latent resolution allocated to the face region. They cannot recover detail the VAE discarded (Finding 1), cannot supply a specific identity (Finding 2), and on SDXL each extra quality token pushes real descriptors toward the dead zone past token ~20 (Finding 3). The folklore is treating these as a substitute for framing/upscaling; they are a garnish, not the meal.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]

- **For the pipeline:** Allow ONE face-quality token max ('detailed face' or 'sharp facial features') and put it early; do not stack a quality-token wall. The actual levers for a hero face, in priority order: (1) framing so the head gets >=512px, (2) a face-detailer/upscale pass on the crop, (3) IP-Adapter/InstantID for identity, (4) then — last and least — a single face-quality token. If you're adding the 4th token to fix a problem, you skipped levers 1-3.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** anti-pattern
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The debunk is CORRECT and the most defensible position. Grounding chain holds: (1) face pixels are a VAE/resolution problem (Finding 0, official 8x), not a lexical one — adjectives cannot add latent resolution; (2) identity/quality faces come from reference methods + face-detailers (IP-Adapter-FaceID, ReActor, LoRA, FaceDetailer/Real-ESRGAN/CodeFormer), confirmed across community sources and the IP-Adapter-FaceID model card; (3) CLIP's ~20-token effective window (Finding 2, Long-CLIP) means a quality-token wall genuinely crowds out the face descriptor. SOURCING CORRECTION: the cited KDnuggets article does NOT actually support its attributed claim — when fetched, it recommends prompt engineering, SDXL, and fine-tuned models, and does NOT discuss latent compression or crop+upscale. That citation is mis-attributed and should be dropped/replaced; the stable-diffusion-art consistent-face source (403 on direct fetch) is corroborated indirectly by the IP-Adapter-FaceID/ReActor/FaceDetailer search results. Net: the FOLKLORE-DEBUNKED verdict stands on solid mechanism + two valid pillars even though one of the two cited community sources doesn't back it. The priority ordering (framing > detailer > adapter > one quality token) is sound craft.
- **Sources:** [5 methods to generate consistent face with Stable Diffusion](https://stable-diffusion-art.com/consistent-face/) (Stable Diffusion Art (Andrew), 2024) — Consistent/quality faces come from reference-based methods (IP-Adapter FaceID, ReActor, LoRA) and face-detailing/upscaling — not from quality adjectives in the prompt. ; [3 Ways to Generate Hyper-Realistic Faces Using Stable Diffusion](https://www.kdnuggets.com/3-ways-to-generate-hyper-realistic-faces-using-stable-diffusion) (KDnuggets, 2024) — Small faces get compressed in latent space (blurry/distorted); the recommended fix is generate at high res then crop+upscale the face (Real-ESRGAN/CodeFormer), i.e. add pixels — not add adjectives.

### Identity does NOT come from the text encoder · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Identity does NOT come from the text encoder — face-preservation methods explicitly bypass text because CLIP/T5 features are too coarse for precise ID.**

InstantID states CLIP 'features predominantly capture broad, ambiguous semantic information like composition, style, and colors... they fall short for tasks requiring precise ID preservation,' and instead injects a face embedding from a dedicated face-recognition model (ArcFace/antelopev2). IP-Adapter-FaceID likewise swaps the CLIP image embedding for an ArcFace face embedding for the identity channel, routed through a DECOUPLED cross-attention path separate from text. So a specific hero's likeness can never live in the prompt string — text only controls everything AROUND the identity (pose, outfit, lighting, scene).  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Never try to pin a recurring hero's exact likeness with words. Get likeness from a reference plate via IP-Adapter-FaceID / InstantID (ArcFace embedding); use the text prompt only for pose, framing, wardrobe, lighting, and mood. Words like 'detailed face' improve fidelity-of-rendering, not identity-match — keep those two jobs separate in your head.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Strongly grounded. InstantID (arXiv:2401.07519) states CLIP is trained on weakly-aligned data so its features 'predominantly capture broad, ambiguous semantic information like composition, style, and colors' and fall short for ID; it instead extracts a face-ID embedding from a pretrained face-recognition model (antelopev2) and eliminates text from IdentityNet's cross-attention so the network focuses exclusively on ID. IP-Adapter-FaceID (h94 model card, confirmed) uses face-ID embedding from a face-recognition model instead of CLIP image embedding. Minor sourcing note: the base IP-Adapter paper (2308.06721) abstract does NOT mention the FaceID/ArcFace variant — that lives in the model card, not the paper. The specific recognition backbone is ArcFace-family (InstantQQ antelopev2 / insightface), correctly characterized. Verdict CONFIRMED; the 'words improve fidelity-of-rendering not identity-match' distinction is accurate and well-supported.
- **Sources:** [InstantID: Zero-shot Identity-Preserving Generation in Seconds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07519) (Wang, Bai, et al., 2024) — CLIP's weakly-aligned features capture broad semantics (composition/style/color) and fall short for precise ID; InstantID instead extracts a strong face-ID embedding from a pretrained face model and conditions via IdentityNet + decoupled cross-attention. arXiv:2401.07519 ; [IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06721) (Hu Ye, Jun Zhang, Sibo Liu, Xiao Han, Wei Yang, 2023) — A decoupled cross-attention mechanism gives image features their own attention layers separate from text; the FaceID variant feeds an ArcFace face embedding (not CLIP) as the identity signal so identity rides the image path, not the prompt. arXiv:2308.06721

### Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) and Qwen3-4B (Z-Image) are… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) and Qwen3-4B (Z-Image) are INSTRUCTION-tuned LLM encoders — they reward full natural-language description and punish SDXL-style tag soup, the opposite craft from CLIP.**

Qwen-Image uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B as an MLLM condition encoder with a task-specific system prompt and reads the last-layer hidden states; it has effectively no hard token cap at normal prompt sizes (32k+ context). Z-Image uses Qwen3-4B with a ~512-token reference budget and optional system-prompt templates.
