Both parse syntax and clause structure, so a coherent sentence ('a weathered swordswoman, mid-30s, with a scar across her left brow and tied-back grey-streaked hair, facing the viewer') outperforms comma-separated tags. The face still has to win pixels (Finding 1), but the encoder itself can follow a sentence-level description of the face.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** For Qwen-Image / Z-Image, write the face as a complete, well-ordered SENTENCE up front, not tags: state framing first ('a close-up portrait of...' or 'a full-body shot of, head clearly visible,'), then the specific facial features as a clause. Keep total under ~512 tokens for Z-Image. You CAN use grammar here — but still convert lore to depictable features (Finding 4 applies to all LLM encoders too).
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen-VL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Encoder facts CONFIRMED: Qwen-Image (arXiv:2508.02324) uses Qwen2.5-VL as an MLLM condition encoder with tailored system prompts per task; Qwen2.5-VL is an instruction-tuned vision-language model. Z-Image (arXiv:2511.22699, Tongyi-MAI, Nov 2025) uses the lightweight Qwen3-4B as text encoder in a single-stream S3-DiT/MM-DiT concatenating text + visual-semantic + VAE tokens, trained exclusively with Qwen3-4B. CORRECTION/CAUTION: '~512 tokens for Z-Image' is UNVERIFIED — neither the Z-Image paper nor community sources I found state a 512-token cap for Qwen3-4B in this pipeline (Qwen3-4B's own context is far larger, 32K+); 512 appears to be carried over from FLUX-T5 folklore and should not be asserted as Z-Image's limit. The qualitative claim that instruction-tuned LLM encoders reward well-formed natural language over tag soup is directionally true and consistent with how MLLM encoders + prompt-rewriters work, but is craft/best-practice, not a quantified finding in the cited papers. CONFIRMED on encoder identity + natural-language orientation; the 512-token number is the one fact to drop or flag.
- **Sources:** [Qwen-Image Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.02324) (Qwen Team, Alibaba, 2025) — Qwen-Image uses Qwen2.5-VL as an MLLM condition encoder with tailored system prompts per task (T2I/TI2I), using last-layer hidden states as the text representation. arXiv:2508.02324 ; [Z-Image: An Efficient Image Generation Foundation Model with Single-Stream Diffusion Transformer](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.22699) (Z-Image Team, Tongyi MAI, Alibaba, 2025) — Z-Image employs the lightweight Qwen3-4B as text encoder in a single-stream MM-DiT where text, visual-semantic and VAE tokens are concatenated; the model is trained exclusively with Qwen3-4B. arXiv:2511.22699

### Reference-conditioning (IP-Adapter/FaceID/InstantID) runs… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Reference-conditioning (IP-Adapter/FaceID/InstantID) runs on a SEPARATE cross-attention path from text and can be weighted independently — face strength is a knob, not a word.**

IP-Adapter's decoupled cross-attention adds dedicated image-feature attention layers parallel to the text layers; InstantID adds IdentityNet (face embedding as 'strong semantic' + 5 facial landmarks as 'weak spatial' control). Both expose an adapter/conditioning scale. This means likeness fidelity is controlled by the adapter weight and the landmark map, fully decoupled from prompt wording — you can crank face fidelity without touching the text, and over-cranking InstantID landmarks over-constrains pose (loss of editability), which is why it uses only 5 keypoints.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Tune the hero's likeness with the ADAPTER scale (IP-Adapter weight / InstantID IdentityNet strength), not by adding more face adjectives to the prompt. If the face is right but the pose is locked/stiff, lower the InstantID landmark/spatial weight rather than rewording. Keep text doing pose+scene+wardrobe; keep the adapter doing identity; tune them on independent dials.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Strongly grounded. IP-Adapter (arXiv:2308.06721) uses a decoupled cross-attention mechanism with separate attention layers for image vs text features, adding only 22M params, and the image path is independent yet compatible with the text prompt (weightable scale). InstantID (arXiv:2401.07519) imposes strong semantic (face-ID embedding) + WEAK spatial conditions using exactly 5 facial keypoints (2 eyes, 1 nose, 2 mouth corners), deliberately kept weak to preserve editability and avoid over-constraining pose. So 'lower the landmark/spatial weight to unstick a stiff pose, keep adapter doing identity' is exactly the documented design intent. Community practice corroborates (reduce IP-Adapter weight ~0.7, FaceDetailer, OpenPose for pose). CONFIRMED — this is one of the best-sourced findings in the set; the independent-dials framing matches the papers precisely.
- **Sources:** [InstantID: Zero-shot Identity-Preserving Generation in Seconds](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07519v1) (Wang, Bai, et al., 2024) — IdentityNet imposes strong semantic (face ID embedding) + weak spatial (5 facial keypoints: eyes, nose, mouth corners) conditions; the weak spatial control deliberately avoids over-constraining pose to preserve editability. arXiv:2401.07519 ; [IP-Adapter: Text Compatible Image Prompt Adapter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06721) (Hu Ye et al., 2023) — Decoupled cross-attention separates image-feature and text-feature attention layers, so image (identity) conditioning is an independent, weightable pathway compatible with the text prompt — only 22M added params. arXiv:2308.06721

### SDXL feeds TWO 77-token CLIP encoders whose token features… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**SDXL feeds TWO 77-token CLIP encoders whose token features are concatenated to [B,77,2048] plus a pooled global embedding — so it is doubly biased toward early, high-salience tokens.**

SDXL runs CLIP-L and OpenCLIP-bigG independently, concatenates their penultimate-layer token features channel-wise into a [B,77,2048] tensor, and ADDITIONALLY conditions on bigG's pooled text embedding. Both encoders share the 77-cap / ~20-effective falloff, and the pooled path summarizes the whole prompt into one vector dominated by salient early tokens. Net: SDXL has the least room of any encoder here for a face to compete with a busy scene description.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL treat the prompt as ~15 high-value tokens, face-first, and offload everything else: put scene/atmosphere mood into the negative-space of a second BREAK chunk, and let likeness come from IP-Adapter/InstantID rather than burning precious early tokens trying to word-paint a specific face. Do not write 60-token SDXL character prompts and expect the face clause at the end to land.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** CLIP · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Architecture CONFIRMED: SDXL uses OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 + CLIP ViT-L/14; per-token embeddings are concatenated along the channel dim to 2048 (1280 from bigG + 768 from L) at 77 tokens -> [B,77,2048], and it additionally conditions on the POOLED text embedding from OpenCLIP bigG (the 1x1280 pooled vector comes only from the second/bigG encoder). All confirmed by the SDXL paper abstract (second encoder, larger cross-attention context) and corroborating community/code sources. CORRECTION on a sub-claim: 'doubly biased toward early, high-salience tokens' is an EXTRAPOLATION, not a paper finding. The ~20-token effective-window evidence is from Long-CLIP studying ONE CLIP; whether concatenating two CLIPs literally 'doubles' early-token bias is not measured anywhere cited — it's a plausible heuristic, treat as FOLKLORE-adjacent reasoning bolted onto a CONFIRMED architecture. The practical advice (short face-first prompt, identity via adapter) is sound; the 'doubly biased' causal story is unproven.
- **Sources:** [SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.01952) (Podell, Englisch, et al., 2023) — SDXL uses OpenCLIP ViT-bigG/14 + CLIP ViT-L/14; token features are concatenated and the model additionally conditions on the pooled text embedding from OpenCLIP. arXiv:2307.01952 ; [Two Text Prompts (Text Encoders) in SDXL 1.0](https://mybyways.com/blog/two-text-prompts-text-encoders-in-sdxl-1-0) (myByways, 2023) — SDXL exposes both encoders and concatenates their per-token embeddings into a [B,77,2048] tensor injected via cross-attention, each encoder still capped at 77 tokens.

### On T5 (FLUX/Chroma), narrative/abstract prose is not 'free… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**On T5 (FLUX/Chroma), narrative/abstract prose is not 'free flavor' — it consumes the conditioning budget and dilutes the depictable tokens, producing generic mush.**

T5-XXL grounds tokens it can map to visual concepts; non-depictable tokens ('worn by grief', 'guarded and steady', the BACKSTORY of why a patch is faded) have no consistent visual referent, so they contribute diffuse, averaged-out attention that pulls the result toward the prior mean. They don't break T5 (it has 512 real, usable positions with no ~20-token collapse), but they crowd out and weaken the concrete visual tokens around them. This is exactly the observed failure: prose-heavy character prompt -> mushy generic result.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Translate every emotional/backstory beat into a DEPICTABLE consequence before it enters a T5 prompt. 'Worn by grief' -> 'hollow cheeks, dark circles under the eyes, downturned mouth'. 'Guarded and steady' -> 'squared shoulders, level gaze, hand resting on sword hilt'. 'Faded patch from an old war' -> 'frayed grey shoulder patch, threadbare edges'. If a clause names no shape, color, posture, texture, or object, cut it.
- **Engine:** T5 · **Base:** T5 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Mechanism grounded. T5 (arXiv:1910.10683) is a pure text-to-text NLP model trained on span-corruption over the C4 corpus with NO visual grounding objective — confirmed by abstract (text-only benchmarks, no image signal). So abstract tokens have no learned visual referent; visual grounding comes only from downstream diffusion training. FLUX uses T5-v1.1-XXL as the detail-carrying encoder (confirmed). Caveat: the strongest version of this claim ('dilutes depictable tokens, produces generic mush') is a reasonable engineering inference from T5's lack of visual grounding plus finite-context attention, NOT a directly-measured result in either cited source — no paper quantifies 'abstract prose -> mush'. The depictable-rewrite craft ('worn by grief' -> 'hollow cheeks, dark circles, downturned mouth') is sound prompt engineering consistent with how T2I grounding works, but is best practice rather than a paper finding. CONFIRMED on mechanism; the 'mush' outcome is plausible-but-not-empirically-cited.
- **Sources:** [Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683) (Raffel et al., 2020) — T5 is a general text-to-text encoder trained on span-corruption over generic text; it has no visual grounding objective, so visual-concept grounding in T2I comes only from the downstream diffusion training — abstract tokens have no learned visual referent. arXiv:1910.10683 ; [FLUX.1-dev: Encoders and Token Limitations](https://medium.com/@lbq999/flux-1-dev-encoders-and-token-limitations-8631c179eaad) (Boqiang Liang, 2024) — FLUX uses CLIP-L (fixed 77 tokens, overall gist) plus T5-v1.1-XXL (up to 512 tokens) as a general-purpose text processor carrying the detailed description; the detail load rides T5.

### T5's full 512-token budget is OPT-IN · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**T5's full 512-token budget is OPT-IN: many runners leave max_sequence_length at 256, silently truncating the back half of a long character prompt.**

FLUX.1-dev/SD3 T5 supports 512 tokens but FLUX.1-schnell caps at 256, and several diffusers code paths default to 256 even on dev. Truncation past max_sequence_length is silent — no error. So a carefully ordered prompt where the face/wardrobe detail sits in the second half can have that half vanish entirely if the runner didn't set 512. Unlike CLIP, there's no effective-length collapse, so the fix is purely 'use the budget you paid for.'  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Explicitly set max_sequence_length=512 in the T5/FLUX/Chroma pipeline, and STILL order the prompt face-first as insurance: subject + face + identity descriptors before scene/lore. On Schnell (256 cap), be ruthless — there is no room for prose at all; depictables only.
- **Engine:** T5 · **Base:** T5 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: EXACT TOKEN FACTS CONFIRMED: FLUX T5 handles up to 512 tokens on FLUX.1-dev and 256 on FLUX.1-schnell; the 77-token limit applies ONLY to the separate CLIP encoder. Full T5 capacity is gated by setting max_sequence_length=512 in the pipeline. One real-world nuance from the HF discussion: in practice long prompts often still take effect past 77 even without explicitly setting the param (the 77 warning is informational, not a hard truncation of T5) — so 'silently truncating the back half' is the documented default-config risk but not guaranteed on every runner. The defensive advice (set 512 explicitly AND order face-first as insurance; Schnell=256 so no room for prose) is correct and conservative. CONFIRMED. Note: schnell's 256 is a genuine half-budget, so the 'be ruthless on Schnell' guidance is well-founded.
- **Sources:** [black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev — Input tokens limited (discussion)](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev/discussions/43) (Black Forest Labs / community, 2024) — FLUX's T5 handles up to 512 tokens (256 on schnell); the 77-token limit applies only to the separate CLIP encoder, and full T5 capacity requires setting max_sequence_length=512. ; [SDXL: Improving Latent Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Synthesis (Podell 2023)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.01952) (Podell et al., 2023) — Establishes the dual-CLIP 77-token conditioning baseline that FLUX/SD3 later supplement with T5's longer window — context for why T5's 512 budget is the 'detail lane'. arXiv:2307.01952

## Negative prompting

### CFG SCALE is the dial on negative strength · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CFG SCALE is the dial on negative strength: higher scale = stronger push away from the negative AND further extrapolation past the positive, which is exactly what produces the 'fried' oversaturated / high-contrast look.**

In eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond), w (the CFG scale) multiplies the whole guidance vector, including the push away from the negative. Raising w makes the negative bite harder but also overshoots: the standard deviation of the resulting latent grows roughly linearly with w. Lin et al. 2023 state plainly 'when w is large, the scale of the resulting x_cfg is very big, causing the image over-exposure problem.' Higher std after VAE decode = blown highlights, crushed blacks, neon over-saturation, plastic skin, halos — the colloquial 'deep-fried' SDXL look. So oversaturation is not a prompt-content bug; it is a direct arithmetic consequence of large w inflating latent magnitude.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Do not 'turn up CFG to make the negative work harder.' For SDXL cel/2.5D art keep CFG 4-7 (start ~5-6); CFG 9+ fries the palette. If you need a stronger negative, ADD a precise negative term rather than raising CFG. Diagnose: if outputs look over-saturated/over-contrasty, your first move is LOWER CFG, not editing the prompt.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen (true-CFG); SDXL is most prone to frying · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources verified. Lin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2305.08891) confirms large guidance weight w inflates the standard deviation/scale of the CFG latent, directly causing the over-exposure/oversaturation problem. The aiphotogenerator CFG guide confirms the practical SDXL ranges: drop CFG ~2 points moving from SD1.5, 7-9 over-sharpens, 5-6 is the practical band. One precision note: 'higher CFG = stronger negative' and 'higher CFG = further past the positive' are the SAME single extrapolation knob w applied to the (cond - uncond/neg) vector — the claim's two-effect framing is correct but they are not independent dials. The diagnostic ('over-saturated => lower CFG first') is exactly what the std-inflation result predicts. PROMPT RULE (keep SDXL cel 4-7, start ~5-6; add a precise negative term rather than raising CFG; diagnose oversaturation by lowering CFG) is well-supported.
- **Sources:** [Common Diffusion Noise Schedules and Sample Steps are Flawed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.08891) (Shanchuan Lin, Bingchen Liu, Jiashi Li, Xiao Yang, 2023) — Large guidance weight w inflates the standard deviation/scale of the CFG latent, directly causing the over-exposure (oversaturation) problem in generated images. arXiv:2305.08891 ; [What Is CFG Scale in Stable Diffusion? Complete Guide](https://www.aiphotogenerator.net/blog/2026/02/what-is-cfg-scale-stable-diffusion) (aiphotogenerator.net, 2026) — Moving from SD1.5 to SDXL one should drop CFG ~2 points; CFG 7-9 on SDXL produces over-sharpened/over-guided images, 5-6 is the practical range.

### CFG scale ranges are model-family-specific and NOT… · `recommended` · community-claim

**CFG scale ranges are model-family-specific and NOT interchangeable — a value that's correct on SDXL fries FLUX and is meaningless on a turbo model.**

Practical ranges, grounded in vendor/community guidance: SDXL-CLIP true CFG ~4-7 (start 5-6; 9+ over-sharpens/saturates — Rescale-CFG ~0.7 if you must go high). Chroma (de-distilled FLUX, T5) runs TRUE CFG and honors negatives, typically ~4-6. Qwen-Image base ~3-5 true CFG. FLUX-dev: real cfg_scale=1, with a SEPARATE distilled 'guidance' embedding ~3.5 (<=3.5 photoreal, 3.5-6 illustration) — this guidance knob is NOT CFG and does not enable negatives. FLUX-schnell / SDXL-Turbo / SDXL-Lightning / LCM / Z-Image-Turbo: cfg_scale=1 fixed, no negatives — use NAG/PAG for control. The common mistake is carrying an SD1.5 CFG~7-9 habit forward, which over-guides SDXL and 'causes chaos in Flux.'  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Set CFG per family in the studio presets, never globally: SDXL 5-6 (cap 7, add RescaleCFG 0.7 above that); Chroma 4-6 with real negatives; Qwen-Image base 3-5; FLUX-dev real-CFG 1 + distilled-guidance 3.5; all turbo/schnell/LCM/Z-Image-Turbo CFG 1 + NAG/PAG for any negative-style control. Don't reuse one number across the rig — wrong CFG is the most common cause of both fried and washed-out JRPG art.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all (per-family ranges differ; SDXL-CLIP / Chroma-T5 / Qwen real-CFG vs FLUX/turbo distilled) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources verified. The andreaskuhr FLUX guide confirms FLUX-dev = CFG 1 + no negative prompt + distilled 'Distilled CFG Guidance' ~3.5 (<=3.5 photoreal, 3.5-6 drawings). NOTE: the guide does NOT state the specific 'distilled 3-4 approximates CFG 7' equivalence the source attributes to it — that sub-detail is unsourced folklore-tier, drop it. The aiphotogenerator CFG guide confirms the family-specific ladder verbatim: SD1.5 7-9, SDXL 5-8 (try 5-6), SD3/3.5 4-7, Flux 1 with separate guidance; carrying SD1.5 values into SDXL over-sharpens and into Flux produces 'a blown-out, artifacts-heavy mess'; ranges must drop with newer architectures. This fully grounds the core claim. The per-family preset table in the PROMPT RULE (SDXL 5-6 cap 7 +RescaleCFG 0.7 above; Qwen base 3-5; FLUX-dev real-CFG 1 + distilled 3.5; all turbo/schnell/LCM CFG 1 + NAG/PAG) is consistent with the verified sources and the other findings; treat the Chroma 4-6 and Qwen 3-5 numbers as reasonable community defaults rather than source-verified here.
- **Sources:** [Flux guidance vs CFG / distilled guidance scale 3.5 guidance](https://andreaskuhr.com/en/flux-ai-guide.html) (andreaskuhr.com; sd-webui-forge discussion #981, 2024) — FLUX-dev: set CFG=1, no negative prompt, use the distilled 'Distilled CFG Guidance' (~3.5; <=3.5 photoreal, 3.5-6 drawings); a distilled guidance of 3-4 approximates what CFG 7 did in older models. ; [What Is CFG Scale in Stable Diffusion? Complete Guide](https://www.aiphotogenerator.net/blog/2026/02/what-is-cfg-scale-stable-diffusion) (aiphotogenerator.net, 2026) — Carrying SD1.5 CFG 7-9 into SDXL over-guides/over-sharpens (use 5-6) and 'causes chaos in Flux'; CFG ranges are family-specific and must be lowered moving to newer architectures.

### Distilled/turbo models ignore negative prompts because… · `recommended` · community-claim

**Distilled/turbo models ignore negative prompts because guidance is baked into a SINGLE forward pass — there is no second (unconditional/negative) branch for the negative to occupy.**

Guidance distillation (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning, LCM, Z-Image-Turbo) trains the student to reproduce, in one forward pass, what a teacher produced with a full CFG two-pass extrapolation. FLUX-dev does this by feeding the guidance value itself as a conditioning embedding (guidance_embeds=true) rather than running two passes; FLUX-schnell drops it entirely. Practically these models run at effective cfg_scale=1, where eps_guided = eps_uncond + 1*(eps_cond - eps_uncond) = eps_cond — the uncond/negative term mathematically vanishes. There is literally no negative branch being evaluated, so a negative_prompt string is inert (often silently accepted and discarded by the UI). Running a real CFG>1 on these models doubles compute AND breaks the distilled output, which is why guides say 'set CFG=1, do not use a negative prompt' for FLUX-dev/schnell.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** On Z-Image-Turbo, FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning, LCM: stop writing negative prompts — they do nothing. Put ALL steering in the POSITIVE prompt (describe the flat cel look you WANT, not the realism you don't). If a UI lets you raise CFG on a turbo model, leave it at 1; raising it fries the image and slows generation for no benefit.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Z-Image · **Base:** distilled-turbo (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning, LCM, Z-Image-Turbo) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Mechanism confirmed, with a precision fix. The NAG paper (arXiv:2505.21179) confirms CFG fails under aggressive step-compression/distillation because positive and negative branch predictions diverge and few-step distilled models do not run dual-branch CFG, so negative guidance is unavailable — this directly grounds the 'no second branch' claim. The andreaskuhr FLUX guide (verified) states verbatim that FLUX-dev is distilled, 'set the CFG scale to 1 and go without a negative prompt,' confirming the practical no-op. IMPORTANT NUANCE the claim slightly overstates: FLUX-dev and turbo models are not all identical. FLUX-dev uses guidance DISTILLATION (a guidance value fed as a conditioning input, guidance_embeds=true) — it genuinely runs one branch. SDXL-Turbo/Lightning/LCM are STEP-distilled; many UIs still technically run a CFG pass but at the recommended CFG=1 the (cond-uncond) term is multiplied by ~0, so the negative is effectively inert. Either way the practical advice holds: negatives do nothing useful. The cited FLUX issue #63 only contains the QUESTION (guidance_embeds true/false), not the recommendation — that specific source does NOT substantiate the CFG=1/no-negative guidance; the andreaskuhr guide and NAG paper carry the claim. PROMPT RULE (put all steering in the positive, leave CFG at 1 on turbo/distilled) is correct.
- **Sources:** [Flux AI guide / guidance_embeds vs CFG explanation](https://github.com/black-forest-labs/flux/issues/63) (andreaskuhr.com; black-forest-labs flux issue #63, 2024) — FLUX-dev carries guidance_embeds=true (guidance value fed as a conditioning input, single pass); FLUX-schnell has it false. Recommended usage is CFG=1 with no negative prompt and a separate distilled-guidance scale (~3.5), because true two-pass CFG is not what these models were trained to run. ; [Normalized Attention Guidance (motivation section)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21179) (Chen et al., 2025) — CFG fails under aggressive sampling-step compression / distillation because positive and negative branch predictions diverge and few-step distilled models do not run the dual-branch CFG, so negative guidance is unavailable. arXiv:2505.21179

### The fix for high-CFG frying is Rescale-CFG (a.k.a. guidance… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**The fix for high-CFG frying is Rescale-CFG (a.k.a. guidance rescale / dynamic thresholding), not a better negative prompt — it renormalizes the latent's std back down after CFG.**

Lin et al. 2023 compute the per-image std of the pure-conditional prediction (sigma_pos) and the std of the over-inflated CFG prediction (sigma_cfg), then rescale: x_rescaled = x_cfg * (sigma_pos / sigma_cfg), and blend x_final = phi*x_rescaled + (1-phi)*x_cfg. This pulls the latent magnitude back to a sane range so high CFG keeps its prompt adherence WITHOUT the over-exposure. They report w=7.5, phi=0.7 'works great,' with phi in [0.5, 0.75] looking appealing. Saharia et al.'s dynamic thresholding does the analogous clamp for pixel-space; Rescale-CFG is the latent-space version exposed in ComfyUI as the 'RescaleCFG' node and in diffusers as the guidance_rescale argument.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** When you genuinely need high CFG (e.g. pushing a hard style at CFG 8-10), enable RescaleCFG/guidance_rescale ~0.7 instead of accepting blown-out art. This lets you keep negative-prompt strength high while killing the deep-fried palette. It is a sampler/pipeline setting, not a prompt edit — bake it into the studio's SDXL/Chroma generation preset.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen (true-CFG); does NOT help distilled/turbo models that run no CFG · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Verified against full text. Lin et al. 2023 (ar5iv 2305.08891) confirms the exact formulas: sigma_pos = std(x_pos), sigma_cfg = std(x_cfg); x_rescaled = x_cfg * (sigma_pos/sigma_cfg); x_final = phi*x_rescaled + (1-phi)*x_cfg; recommended w=7.5 and phi=0.7 with the [0.5, 0.75] range called most visually appealing. This is a pipeline/sampler operation applied to the latent, not a prompt edit — matching the RescaleCFG node lineage in ComfyUI (the dynamic-thresholding repo is the well-known reference implementation of the same family). PROMPT RULE (enable RescaleCFG/guidance_rescale ~0.7 when you genuinely need high CFG, bake into the studio preset) is accurate and correctly classified as a setting rather than a prompt change.
- **Sources:** [Common Diffusion Noise Schedules and Sample Steps are Flawed (Sec. guidance rescale)](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2305.08891) (Shanchuan Lin, Bingchen Liu, Jiashi Li, Xiao Yang, 2023) — x_rescaled = x_cfg*(sigma_pos/sigma_cfg); x_final = phi*x_rescaled + (1-phi)*x_cfg; empirically w=7.5, phi=0.7 works great with phi in [0.5,0.75] appealing — fixes over-exposure at high guidance for both latent and pixel diffusion. arXiv:2305.08891 ; [sd-dynamic-thresholding (Saharia-style clamp / latent CFG rescale implementation)](https://github.com/mcmonkeyprojects/sd-dynamic-thresholding) (mcmonkeyprojects, 2023) — Reference implementation of dynamic thresholding / CFG rescaling that mitigates the saturation effect of high CFG; the technique generalized into the RescaleCFG node used in ComfyUI.

### copy-pasted 50-80 word negative blocklists ('worst quality,… · `recommended` · community-claim

**FOLKLORE: copy-pasted 50-80 word negative blocklists ('worst quality, low quality, jpeg artifacts, ugly, bad hands...') are mostly cargo cult — token competition dilutes each term and several terms are inert.**

Mechanically, the negative prompt is a single embedding; cramming dozens of concepts in spreads the limited 'avoidance' across all of them, so each term gets a weak directional contribution (and on CLIP models, past 77 tokens the tail is truncated entirely). Terms like 'worst quality/low quality' only do anything if the base/finetune was captioned with those literal phrases (true for many SD1.5/anime models, largely NOT for SDXL base, FLUX, Qwen, Z-Image) — otherwise they are near-random directions. Community testing repeatedly shows SDXL/SD3.5 often improve with SHORTER negatives, and removing irrelevant terms lets the model focus avoidance energy on the ones that matter. The mathematically reliable lever is weighting/embeddings, not word count.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Delete the inherited mega-negative. Use 3-8 targeted terms max, each one a concept actually present-and-unwanted in YOUR positive's direction (for 2.5D cel art: 'photorealistic, 3d render, photograph, blurry'). Drop 'worst quality/low quality' on SDXL/FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image unless you verified that finetune was trained on those tags. If a term needs to bite harder, weight it ((term:1.3)) rather than adding ten cousins of it. Audit the studio's preset negatives — most are probably dead weight.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all true-CFG models; the 77-token truncation point is SDXL-CLIP-specific (T5/Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL encoders have much longer windows) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Verified as a debunk of the mega-negative ritual, with a calibration note. The zeroskillai guide explicitly calls 80-word negative lists a 'cargo cult ritual' and gives the dilution mechanism verbatim: 'If you list 50 negative terms, the model treats them all with roughly equal avoidance strength... nothing gets properly suppressed,' and identifies weights/embeddings as the real lever. The aiphotogenerator negative-prompt guide independently confirms SDXL/SD3.5 want 'shorter, more targeted' negatives and that 'the model spreads its avoidance energy thin.' HONEST CALIBRATION (per the 'be hard on mega-negative efficacy' mandate): these are strong-community sources, not controlled ablations — there is NO peer-reviewed study quantifying that a 50-term negative is worse than a 5-term one. The attention-dilution argument is mechanistically plausible (all terms share the same fixed-length conditioning, and softmax attention does spread mass) and is the field consensus, but the 'several terms are inert' sub-claim is model-specific: 'worst quality/low quality' DO bite on finetunes literally trained on booru quality tags (many anime SD1.5/SDXL/Pony/Illustrious models), and are dead weight on base SDXL/FLUX/Qwen — exactly as the prompt rule says. So the claim is correctly directional, not a measured law. PROMPT RULE (3-8 targeted terms, drop worst/low quality unless the finetune was trained on them, weight rather than pile on cousins, audit studio presets) is the correct operational takeaway and is itself the strongest part.
- **Sources:** [Stop Typing 'Ugly': Advanced Negative Prompt Guide (Embeddings & Weights)](https://zeroskillai.com/advanced-negative-prompt-guide-weights-embeddings/) (zeroskillai.com, 2026) — Long copy-pasted negatives are a 'cargo cult ritual'; every term competes for the model's attention, so 50-term lists spread avoidance thin — removing irrelevant terms often improves results, and weighting/embeddings are the real lever. ; [Negative Prompts Explained: What They Are, How They Work](https://www.aiphotogenerator.net/blog/2026/02/negative-prompts-stable-diffusion-guide) (aiphotogenerator.net, 2026) — SDXL and SD3.5 need less aggressive negative prompting than SD1.5; some SDXL models get worse with long negative lists — shorter, targeted negatives perform better.

### NAG (Normalized Attention Guidance) restores real… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**NAG (Normalized Attention Guidance) restores real negative-prompt control on distilled/turbo models by doing the extrapolation in ATTENTION space instead of in the noise prediction.**

NAG (Chen et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.21179) is training-free. Inside attention, it computes positive and negative attention features Z+ and Z-, extrapolates Z_tilde = Z+ + scale*(Z+ - Z-), then applies L1-based normalization (a tau clamp that constrains how far Z_tilde may deviate from Z+) and alpha-blends back toward Z+. The normalization is the key trick: naive attention extrapolation drifts out-of-manifold (the same divergence that kills CFG in few-step models), and the L1 clamp keeps it stable. NAG is validated on FLUX-schnell (4-step), FLUX-dev, SDXL-Turbo/DMD2, SD3.5-Large-Turbo, and Wan2.1 video; on FLUX-schnell 4-step it improves CLIP score +2.1 and cuts FID 18% vs no guidance. Recommended nag_scale ~5 for FLUX/SD3.5-Turbo and ~3 for SDXL-DMD2, with guidance_scale left at 0.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** If the studio wants negative-prompt control on Z-Image-Turbo / FLUX-schnell-class models, add the NAG node (ComfyUI) or NAG-enabled pipeline and put suppressions (e.g. 'blurry, realistic, watermark, extra fingers') in nag_negative_prompt with nag_scale ~3-5. This is the ONLY mechanically valid way to get negative-like control on a distilled model — a plain negative_prompt field on those models is still a no-op.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Z-Image · **Base:** distilled-turbo (FLUX-schnell, FLUX-dev, SDXL-Turbo/DMD2, SD3.5-Turbo, Z-Image-Turbo-class) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources verified. Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.21179) confirms NAG is a training-free mechanism applying extrapolation in attention space with L1-based normalization and refinement, restoring negative guidance where CFG collapses under step-compression; works across UNet/DiT, few-step/multi-step, image/video. The official ChenDarYen repo confirms the recommended configs: FLUX(-Schnell) nag_scale=5.0/guidance_scale=0; SD3.5-Turbo nag_scale=5/guidance_scale=0; SDXL+DMD2 nag_scale=3/guidance_scale=0 — i.e. NAG supplies the negative branch the distilled model lacks. The abstract did not surface the exact '+2.1 CLIP / -18% FID on Flux-Schnell 4-step' numbers (it lists CLIP/FID/PFID/ImageReward improvements generically), so treat those specific deltas as UNVERIFIED-from-abstract but plausible and not load-bearing. PROMPT RULE (use NAG node, put suppressions in nag_negative_prompt, nag_scale ~3-5, knowing plain negative_prompt is a no-op on distilled models) is sound.
- **Sources:** [Normalized Attention Guidance: Universal Negative Guidance for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21179) (Dar-Yen Chen et al., 2025) — Training-free attention-space extrapolation of Z+/Z- with L1 normalization and alpha-blending restores stable negative guidance in few-step/distilled regimes; on Flux-Schnell 4-step it gives +2.1 CLIP and -18% FID vs no guidance. arXiv:2505.21179 ; [Normalized-Attention-Guidance (official implementation, recommended values)](https://github.com/ChenDarYen/Normalized-Attention-Guidance) (ChenDarYen (GitHub), 2025) — Example configs: FLUX nag_scale=5.0/guidance_scale=0; SD3.5-Turbo nag_scale=5/guidance_scale=0; SDXL+DMD2 nag_scale=3/guidance_scale=0 — demonstrating NAG supplies the negative branch the distilled model lacks.

### A negative prompt is not a 'filter · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**A negative prompt is not a 'filter' — it literally replaces the unconditioned branch of the CFG equation, so generation is pushed along the vector AWAY from the negative embedding.**

Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans 2022) jointly trains a conditional and an unconditional (null-token) denoiser. At each sampling step the guided noise prediction is the linear extrapolation eps_guided = eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond). A negative prompt swaps eps_uncond for eps_neg = eps(x, c-), giving eps_guided = eps_cond + w*(eps_cond - eps_neg). Geometrically the model takes the vector from the negative embedding to the positive embedding and walks PAST the positive by factor w. So the negative is not subtracted feature-by-feature; it just redefines the origin the model extrapolates away from. This is why a negative prompt's effect is relative to the positive — adding the same word to BOTH prompts cancels it out, and a negative term only bites when it differs from the positive direction.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Treat the negative as the 'anchor you flee from,' not a blocklist. Only put things in the negative that are genuinely absent from your positive intent (e.g. 'photographic, 3d render, realistic skin' to defend a flat 2.5D JRPG cel look). Never duplicate a concept in both positive and negative — it nets to zero. Keep it short and directional.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen (all un-distilled / true-CFG models) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Mechanism confirmed. Ho & Salimans 2022 (arXiv:2207.12598) verified: CFG jointly trains a conditional and unconditional denoiser and combines their score estimates, no external classifier; the guided prediction is the standard linear extrapolation eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond). When a negative prompt is supplied, it occupies the 'unconditional' slot of that equation, so generation is steered away from the negative embedding rather than being filtered out post-hoc. CAVEAT ON THE CITED OFFICIAL-DOCS SOURCE: the diffusers 'weighted_prompts' page (the second source) has been rewritten and no longer states that negative_prompt_embeds occupies the unconditional branch — it now only mentions the argument exists. The mechanistic claim is independently corroborated by the aiphotogenerator negative-prompt guide, which states verbatim: 'Adding a negative prompt replaces the unconditional prediction with a conditional one based on your negative terms.' So the CLAIM is well-grounded; only the specific HF-docs citation is stale. PROMPT RULE is sound (anchor-you-flee-from framing, no concept duplicated in both fields, short/directional) and follows directly from the vector mechanics.
- **Sources:** [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Jonathan Ho, Tim Salimans, 2022) — Guidance is performed by a pure generative model that jointly trains conditional and unconditional denoisers; the guided score is a linear extrapolation eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond), no external classifier needed. arXiv:2207.12598 ; [diffusers prompting / negative_prompt_embeds + negative_pooled_prompt_embeds](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/main/en/using-diffusers/weighted_prompts) (Hugging Face, 2024) — Negative prompts are passed as negative_prompt_embeds and occupy the unconditional branch of the CFG computation, confirming the negative replaces the uncond prediction rather than acting as a post-filter.

### PAG (Perturbed-Attention Guidance) is the other… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**PAG (Perturbed-Attention Guidance) is the other distilled-model workaround, but it is a STRUCTURE/quality booster, not a true negative — it needs no negative prompt at all and works even at CFG=1.**

PAG (Ahn et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.17377) creates a deliberately structurally-degraded version of the prediction by replacing selected self-attention maps in the U-Net with an identity matrix, then guides AWAY from that degraded sample. Because the 'thing to avoid' is generated internally (not from a text negative), PAG works in unconditional generation and at guidance_scale=0/1 — exactly the regime where CFG/negatives are dead. diffusers' default pag_scale=3.0 'works well in most cases'; too-high pag_scale itself causes smoother textures and slight saturation (same failure family as CFG). Crucially PAG cannot suppress a SPECIFIC concept (it has no semantic target) — it only repairs anatomy/composition coherence. So for distilled models: use PAG to fix wonky hands/structure, use NAG to suppress a named attribute.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On turbo/distilled JRPG renders with anatomy or composition glitches but no specific thing to ban, enable PAG (pag_scale ~3.0) rather than stacking 'bad anatomy, extra fingers' into a dead negative field. Use PAG for 'make it cleaner/coherent'; reach for NAG only when you must ban a NAMED concept. Don't crank pag_scale past ~4-5 or you reintroduce the saturated look.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** distilled-turbo + un-distilled SDXL (diffusers PAG supported on SDXL/PixArt pipelines) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources verified. Ahn et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.17377) confirms PAG substitutes selected self-attention maps in the U-Net with an identity matrix to create a structurally degraded sample and guides away from it, improving quality in BOTH unconditional and conditional settings without a negative prompt or extra training. The diffusers PAG doc confirms pag_scale=3.0 is the official-demo default that works in most cases, that PAG works well for unconditional generation (guidance_scale=0), and that overly large pag_scale 'can lead to smoother textures and slight saturation in the images, similarly to CFG.' This fully supports the claim's framing of PAG as a coherence/structure booster (not a concept ban) and the warning against cranking pag_scale. PROMPT RULE (PAG for 'make it cleaner/coherent', NAG when you must ban a NAMED concept; don't push pag_scale past ~4-5) is well-grounded.
- **Sources:** [Self-Rectifying Diffusion Sampling with Perturbed-Attention Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17377) (Donghoon Ahn et al., 2024) — Substituting self-attention maps with an identity matrix yields a structurally-degraded sample; guiding away from it improves quality in BOTH conditional and unconditional settings without a negative prompt or extra training. arXiv:2403.17377 ; [diffusers — Perturbed-Attention Guidance](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/pag) (Hugging Face, 2024) — pag_scale=3.0 is the official-demo default and works in most cases; PAG works well for unconditional generation (guidance_scale=0) and overly-large pag_scale causes smoother textures and slight saturation like CFG.

### Distilled/turbo models (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell,… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Distilled/turbo models (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning) have no true CFG, so the negative field is dead weight -- and a non-empty negative can actively cost speed for zero benefit.**

Guidance distillation bakes the guidance behavior into the weights; inference runs a single conditional pass with a 'distilled guidance' scalar (FLUX-dev default ~3.5), not the two-pass cond/uncond subtraction CFG requires. With CFG=1 there is no uncond/negative branch to substitute, so the negative is ignored by design (Forge greys out the negative field at CFG=1). Schnell doesn't even use guidance. Re-enabling real CFG to force a negative (e.g. via dynamic-thresholding hacks or pseudo-negative nodes) roughly doubles step cost and breaks the distillation the model was trained for. (This restates the established rule; the actionable payoff is the cleanup instruction.)  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** On FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning: leave the negative field EMPTY. Put avoid-intent into the positive as presence-language ('clean uncluttered background, sharp focus'). Do not wire CFG-restoring negative hacks for production art -- they ~2x cost for marginal gain.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Z-Image · **Base:** distilled-turbo (FLUX-dev, FLUX-schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. Forge discussion #981 (lllyasviel) verified VERBATIM: 'Flux-dev is a distilled model. It is recommended to set CFG=1 and then do not use negative prompts. Using Distilled CFG Guidance instead (default 3.5)... if CFG=1, the UI of negative prompt will be greyed out.' The ~2x cost claim verified at the NeuralSamurAI FluxPseudoNegativePrompt repo: negatives via CFG restoration make 'generation time double more or less.' So 'empty negative on distilled models + put avoid-intent into the positive as presence-language' is correct and well-sourced. Minor scope honesty: the cited sources directly cover FLUX dev/schnell only. SDXL-Turbo/Lightning and Z-Image-Turbo are correctly grouped by the same distillation/low-CFG mechanism, but that grouping is inference, not separately cited -- it's a safe inference (turbo/lightning run at CFG~1) but flag it as 'by mechanism' rather than 'each model independently sourced.'
- **Sources:** [BitsandBytes Guidelines and Flux (Forge): distilled guidance, CFG=1, negative greyed out](https://github.com/lllyasviel/stable-diffusion-webui-forge/discussions/981) (lllyasviel / Forge, 2024) — FLUX dev/schnell are distilled; set CFG=1 with no negative prompt and use Distilled CFG Guidance (~3.5); the negative-prompt UI greys out at CFG=1. ; [FLUX Pseudo Negative / dynamic-thresholding negative for FLUX](https://github.com/NeuralSamurAI/ComfyUI-FluxPseudoNegativePrompt) (NeuralSamurAI / community, 2024) — FLUX needs custom nodes to fake negatives because it doesn't natively support them; applying real negatives via CFG restoration significantly increases generation time.

### long copy-pasted 'cargo' negatives ('deformed, ugly, poorly… · `recommended` · community-claim

**FOLKLORE: long copy-pasted 'cargo' negatives ('deformed, ugly, poorly drawn, bad anatomy, extra limbs, lowres, jpeg artifacts...') help a GOOD positive. In practice they mostly flatten variety and on modern models can make output WORSE.**

Each negative token spends a slice of the same finite avoidance budget, so a 30-50 item list spreads suppression thin and, worse, broad terms bleed via concept neighborhoods (negating 'moss' also dims 'grass'/'green'; negating 'ugly' dims whole aesthetic regions), collapsing diversity. arXiv:2406.02965 and the SD3.5/SDXL practitioner consensus both report that removing the negative sometimes IMPROVES complex scenes, and that newer models (SDXL, SD3.5, FLUX, Qwen) need far less or no negative than SD1.5 did. The empirical bottom line: negatives are a corrective for a SPECIFIC observed defect, not a quality multiplier on an already-good prompt. The cargo list is a ritual carried over from SD1.5.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Start with an EMPTY negative. Generate, inspect, and add ONE depictable token only for a defect you actually see. Never paste a stock cargo list. If you're on SDXL/Chroma and the positive is strong, 0-5 negative tokens is the ceiling.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5 (true-CFG models); cargo lists are pure folklore on distilled/Qwen) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The folklore-debunk is itself well-grounded -- correctly flips the cargo-cult myth. Ban et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) supplies the mechanism: negatives are targeted concept-deletion via mutual cancellation, NOT a general quality boost -- so a generic block has no principled reason to help. Independent corroboration of 'long lists hurt on modern models': Civitai SDXL embedding creators report 'SDXL no longer needs a long list... some models even perform worse'; SD3.5 guidance reports removing negatives sometimes IMPROVES complex scenes; high-CFG + long negatives causes oversaturation/artifact loss. ATTRIBUTION FIX: the prompt sources Ban et al. for 'human-provided negatives frequently fail to improve image quality' -- the paper's verified claim is narrower (negatives WORK as targeted deletion; they are not a quality booster), it does not assert humans 'frequently fail.' That specific framing belongs to the Sider.ai community blog (which I could not fetch -- 403), so cite the failure-to-improve point as community + Civitai, not as a Ban et al. result. Conclusion stands: CONFIRMED.
- **Sources:** [Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02965) (Ban et al., 2024) — Human-provided negatives frequently fail to improve image quality; effect is concept-deletion of specific targets, not a general quality boost. arXiv:2406.02965 ; [Negative Prompts in Stable Diffusion: Guardrails or Guesswork?](https://sider.ai/blog/ai-tools/negative-prompts-in-stable-diffusion-guardrails-or-guesswork) (Sider.ai, 2026) — Cargo-cult negative lists tell the model 'be boring', reduce variety, and on SD3.5/SDXL removing negatives sometimes improves complex scenes; SDXL needs far shorter negatives than SD1.5.

### MINIMAL DEFENSIBLE DEFAULTS per family · `recommended` · community-claim

**MINIMAL DEFENSIBLE DEFAULTS per family: short depictable lists only where true CFG exists; empty everywhere distillation killed it. High-CFG SDXL also needs CFG-rescale, not more negatives, to fix burn.**

Synthesizing the above into shippable defaults for a 2.5D JRPG character pipeline. SDXL (CLIP, true CFG): default negative = 'lowres, blurry, watermark, text, signature, extra fingers, jpeg artifacts' -- 5-8 depictable defects, comma tags; if pushing CFG high for adherence, add CFG-rescale (Lin et al 2023, arXiv:2305.08891) ~0.7 to kill oversaturation rather than fighting burn with negatives. Chroma / FLUX-base (T5, true CFG): short prose negative 'blurry, low-detail, watermark or text overlay, deformed hands' -- one clause, not a tag dump. FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning: EMPTY negative, steer positively. Qwen-Image: empty-string ' ' negative, rely on positive + positive_magic. Always start nearer empty and add per-defect.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Ship these defaults: SDXL -> 'lowres, blurry, watermark, text, extra fingers, jpeg artifacts' (+ CFG-rescale 0.7 if CFG>7); Chroma/FLUX-base -> short clause 'blurry low-detail image, watermark or text, deformed hands'; FLUX-dev/schnell + Z-Image-Turbo + SDXL-Turbo -> empty; Qwen-Image -> empty string. Then trim/extend per observed defect.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all (per-family split) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded, with the burn-fix being the strongest single piece. CFG-rescale: Lin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2305.08891) confirmed -- the paper explicitly proposes rescaling classifier-free guidance to prevent over-exposure; high guidance causes over-exposure/oversaturation and rescaling tames it while preserving direction. So 'use CFG-rescale ~0.7, not more negative tokens, for high-CFG burn' is correctly sourced and is the right architectural fix. The per-family default routing (SDXL short list / FLUX-base short clause / FLUX-dev+turbo empty / Qwen empty string) is consistent with every other verified finding in this set (claims 4,5,6). One honesty note: neurocanvas.net (the cited SDXL-best-practices source) actually ships READY-MADE cargo lists and says 'SDXL does not need long negative lists like SD 1.5' but does NOT teach 'start short, add reactively' -- so that specific 'start short' guidance is better attributed to broader community consensus (Civitai/SD3.5 guides, independently confirmed) than to neurocanvas. The defaults themselves are defensible; trim the over-precise attribution. CONFIRMED.
- **Sources:** [Common Diffusion Noise Schedules and Sample Steps are Flawed (CFG-rescale)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.08891) (Lin, Liu, Li, Yang, 2023) — High guidance causes over-exposure/oversaturation; rescaling CFG by the ratio of conditional to CFG-output std dev preserves direction while taming burn -- the correct fix for high-CFG artifacts, not more negative tokens. arXiv:2305.08891 ; [SDXL Best Practices: Settings, Prompts & Workflows](https://neurocanvas.net/blog/sdxl-best-practices-guide/) (neurocanvas.net, 2025) — SDXL needs short targeted negatives focused on removing specific unwanted elements; start short and add terms only when a specific problem appears in output.

### A negative prompt is a CONCEPT to move away from, not a… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**A negative prompt is a CONCEPT to move away from, not a sentence containing a negation -- put 'hat', not 'no hat'.**

CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022) computes output = uncond + scale*(cond - uncond); negative prompting replaces the uncond branch with the negative embedding, so the sampler is mechanically pushed DOWN the gradient of whatever the negative text encodes. The field already means 'away-from'. Words like 'no'/'without'/'not' are near-meaningless to the image encoders (CLIP has no robust logical negation; T5 spreads attention contextually) so 'no hat' encodes the concepts {no, hat} and the dominant token is 'hat' -- you push away from the negation word's neighborhood while still naming the thing. arXiv:2601.08070 (Semantic Gravity Wells) shows the 'priming' failure mode dominates: explicitly naming the forbidden token in a negation construction is itself the primary risk factor (87.5% of failures), because attention lands on the named target, not the negation cue.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Write bare depictable concept tokens in the negative field: 'hat, sunglasses, blur'. NEVER write 'no hat' or 'without a hat'. The field sign already handles the 'no'.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen-Image base (any model with true CFG) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded. Mechanism source (Ho & Salimans 2022, arXiv:2207.12598) confirmed: CFG combines conditional + unconditional score estimates to trade quality vs diversity. IMPORTANT CAVEAT the verifier flags: that paper does NOT mention negative prompts at all -- substituting a negative for the unconditional branch is a documented community extension, not a finding in the cited paper. The behavioral half is solid from two other verified sources: (a) Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.05375, ICLR'24) confirms negation phrasing in the POSITIVE prompt fails -- models 'struggle to effectively suppress content explicitly requested to be omitted' -- which is the depiction the rule cares about; (b) Rana 2026 (arXiv:2601.08070) is REAL and its numbers (87.5% priming failure; 4.4x suppression asymmetry, 5.2pp vs 22.8pp) verify EXACTLY -- but it studies LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS and forbidden-word text instructions, NOT image diffusion. Citing it as evidence for image negative-prompt behavior is a domain transplant. The conclusion still holds for diffusion via Wang et al., so CONFIRMED, but drop or re-label the Rana citation as cross-domain analogy and stop attributing the 'concept not negation' rule to Ho & Salimans.
- **Sources:** [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Ho & Salimans, 2022) — CFG extrapolates from the unconditional toward the conditional; substituting a negative prompt for the unconditional branch pushes samples away from that description. arXiv:2207.12598 ; [Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08070) (Shailesh Rana, 2026) — Priming failure (87.5% of failures): explicitly naming the forbidden word activates rather than suppresses it; suppression is 4.4x weaker in failures (5.2pp vs 22.8pp drop in target probability). arXiv:2601.08070

### A negative should TARGET a specific observed defect, not… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**A negative should TARGET a specific observed defect, not blindly mirror/oppose the positive -- but it must NOT collide with the positive's own content, or mutual cancellation deletes what you wanted.**

The neutralization mechanism (arXiv:2406.02965) means a negative token cancels the matching positive concept. So mirroring the positive is dangerous: if the positive says 'red cloak' and the negative says 'red', you suppress the cloak's color. Good negatives are ORTHOGONAL to the wanted content -- they name failure modes the model tends to add ('blur, watermark, extra fingers, text'), not attributes you asked for. The exception is deliberate disambiguation: to stop an unwanted reading of an ambiguous positive token, name the unwanted sense in the negative (positive 'crane (bird)', negative 'construction crane'). This is the legitimate 'oppose' use -- opposing an unwanted INTERPRETATION, not opposing your own subject.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Build negatives from observed failure modes orthogonal to your subject, never from words that overlap your positive content. Only 'oppose' the positive to kill a specific wrong reading of an ambiguous token (positive 'bat (animal)' -> negative 'baseball bat').
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen-Image base · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded, and a genuinely useful corollary of the verified mechanism. Ban et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) confirmed: deletion happens via mutual cancellation between matching positive and negative concepts -- so a negative token that overlaps your positive content WILL neutralize that content. This directly supports both halves of the rule: (a) build negatives from observed failure modes orthogonal to the subject; (b) only deliberately 'oppose' the positive to kill a wrong reading of an ambiguous token. Wang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.05375) reinforces the 'target the specific unwanted concept rather than negation phrasing' half. No correction. The 'bat (animal) -> negative baseball bat' disambiguation example is a reasonable application of mutual-cancellation, not separately cited but mechanism-consistent.
- **Sources:** [Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02965) (Ban et al., 2024) — Negatives delete via mutual cancellation with matching positive concepts; a negative token overlapping positive content will neutralize that content. arXiv:2406.02965 ; [Get What You Want, Not What You Don't: Image Content Suppression for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.05375) (Wang et al., 2024) — Documents suppression failure cases ('a man without glasses' still draws glasses), motivating targeting the specific unwanted concept rather than negation phrasing. arXiv:2402.05375

### The negative token must itself be DEPICTABLE (the… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**The negative token must itself be DEPICTABLE (the depictability law applies symmetrically). Abstract negatives like 'low quality', 'bad', 'amateur' do almost nothing.**

Negation works by mutual cancellation in latent space (arXiv:2406.02965): the negative prompt only deletes a concept if that concept has a strong, localizable visual representation whose noise can cancel the positive noise. 'blurry', 'lowres', 'jpeg artifacts', 'watermark', 'extra fingers' are depictable defects -- they map to coherent image features and cancel well. 'low quality'/'bad anatomy'/'masterpiece'(negated) are abstract aesthetic abstractions with no single visual locus, so they smear weak, diffuse pressure and mostly just reduce variety. arXiv:2601.08070 quantifies this: violation probability is predicted by the concept's baseline depictability/probability (P0), violation = sigma(-2.40 + 2.27*P0), 78% of variance -- low-pressure (rare/abstract) concepts the model wasn't going to draw anyway are 'suppressed' trivially (9% violation) while strongly-depicted concepts resist (46%).  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Only put depictable nouns/defects in negatives ('blur', 'watermark', 'text', 'six fingers'). Delete abstract aesthetic words ('low quality', 'bad', 'ugly', 'masterpiece') -- they waste tokens and flatten variety.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all (true-CFG models honor it; distilled models ignore it entirely) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded with a caveat on overreach. Ban et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) confirmed: negatives operate by 'Deletion Through Neutralization' -- mutual cancellation in latent space against a positive concept, i.e. a targeted, localizable feature. A negative only bites when it aligns to a target region, which favors concrete depictable tokens over abstract aesthetic words. Rana 2026's P0/logistic finding (violation prob = sigma(-2.40+2.27*P0), high-pressure concepts resist suppression) verified verbatim but again is LLM-domain, not diffusion -- it supports the 'depictability/pressure matters' intuition by analogy only, not directly. The 'abstract words do ALMOST NOTHING' phrasing slightly overstates: the diffusion literature shows abstract tokens are weak/inconsistent, not provably null, and 'masterpiece'/'low quality' tokens are real learned tags in some booru-trained checkpoints (SD1.5-era) where they do shift output. So: CONFIRMED that depictable >> abstract; soften 'almost nothing' to 'weak and model-dependent.'
- **Sources:** [Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02965) (Ban et al., 2024) — Negative prompts delete concepts via mutual cancellation in latent space; the effect requires the negative concept to align to a target region, i.e. to be a localizable depictable feature. arXiv:2406.02965 ; [Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08070) (Shailesh Rana, 2026) — Violation probability is a logistic function of the concept's baseline probability P0 (78% of variance); high-pressure concepts resist suppression, low-pressure ones are suppressed trivially. arXiv:2601.08070

### Negatives bite LATE in sampling and only after the positive… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Negatives bite LATE in sampling and only after the positive has rendered content -- so a negative cannot pre-empt a defect, it can only correct an emerging one.**

arXiv:2406.02965 measures the timing: positive prompts attend to their content in the first ~4 steps, but negative prompts cannot align to the target region until step ~8+, peaking around step 5 for noun removal and plateauing around step 10 for adjective/quality refinement; they are effectively inert after ~step 11. This is why a negative reliably removes an object that the positive is trying to draw (object cancellation) but is a poor tool for shaping global composition or 'baking in' style -- those decisions are already locked in the first few steps. Practical implication: negatives are a corrective scalpel, not a steering wheel.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Use negatives to remove/clean specific emergent elements (an unwanted object, blur, a watermark), NOT to set composition or style -- do that in the positive. Don't expect a negative to fix something decided in the first 4 steps.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen-Image base · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Strongly grounded -- the single best-sourced finding in the set. Ban et al. 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) full text verified VERBATIM: positive prompt glasses attend 'within the first four steps'; negative-prompt glasses 'cannot attend to the right position until the eighth step'; quantitative peak 'at the 5th step for the noun-based negative prompt'; adjective negatives 'plateau around the 10th'; and 'beyond step 11, applying negative prompts appears ineffective.' Every timestep number in the prompt_rule matches the paper. No correction needed. (One scope note: these step numbers are for the specific sampler/step-count in that paper's experiments and should be read as 'late-window relative' not absolute across all schedulers, but the qualitative law -- negatives correct emergent content, they don't set composition -- is exactly what the paper shows.)
- **Sources:** [Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02965) (Ban et al., 2024) — Positive prompts attend in first 4 steps; negatives cannot align until step ~8, peak at step 5 (nouns) / plateau at step 10 (adjectives), ineffective after step 11. arXiv:2406.02965

### Per-encoder syntax differs · `recommended` · community-claim

**Per-encoder syntax differs: CLIP negatives are comma-separated concept tokens; T5/Qwen2.5-VL negatives should be a short natural descriptive phrase -- and both obey the same 77/512 limits and front-loading as the positive.**

CLIP (SDXL) is a causal, contrastively-trained encoder with a hard 77-token window and an EOS token that hoards semantics; it parses tag-like comma lists well and weights front tokens more, so a CLIP negative is best written as a short comma list of concept tags ('blur, watermark, text'). T5-XXL (Chroma, FLUX-base) and Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen-Image) are sentence-level encoders with spread-out contextual attention and a 512-token window; they read prose, so a T5 negative reads better as a brief grammatical clause ('blurry low-detail background with visible compression artifacts'). The 77/512 token limits and front-loading apply to the negative field exactly as to the positive -- a bloated negative truncates and dilutes just like a bloated positive (arXiv:2504.01137 on cross-token info flow; HF FLUX docs on T5's 512 vs CLIP's 77).  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** CLIP/SDXL negative = comma-separated concept tags, front-loaded, well under 77 tokens. T5/Chroma & Qwen negative = one short descriptive phrase. Keep the most important avoid-concept first in both.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP (tags) vs Chroma-T5 / Qwen (phrase) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded, correctly labeled strong-community. The 77-vs-512 token split is hard-confirmed: FLUX.1-dev HF discussion #43 verified -- 'Flux has a second, T5, text encoder that can handle up to 512 tokens,' CLIP caps at 77 (warning fires but T5 tokens past 77 still generate). Toker et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.01137) verified to support encoder-shape differences: information concentrates in only one or two tokens, items can interfere ('pool by a table' -> pool table), and 'simple interventions at the encoding stage improve alignment' -- consistent with CLIP being sparse/localized vs T5 contextual. CAVEAT: the abstract did NOT surface the specific 'CLIP causal + dominant EOS + dense localized attention vs T5 spread-out sentence-level' phrasing; that characterization is body-level / community synthesis, hence the strong-community (not empirical-paper) grade is the honest one. The practical syntax rule (tags for CLIP, phrase for T5) is sound craft consensus, not a quoted experimental result. Keep as CONFIRMED at strong-community tier; do not upgrade the EOS-dominance specifics to 'proven by Toker.'
- **Sources:** [Follow the Flow: On Information Flow Across Textual Tokens in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.01137) (Toker et al., 2025) — CLIP encodes causally with a dominant EOS token and dense localized attention; T5 produces spread-out contextual attention emphasizing sentence-level semantics -- different prompt shapes suit each. arXiv:2504.01137 ; [FLUX.1-dev input token limit discussion / diffusers T5 vs CLIP](https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev/discussions/43) (Black Forest Labs / HF, 2024) — The 77-token limit is the CLIP encoder's; the T5-XXL main encoder handles 512 tokens.

### Qwen-Image is the trap · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Qwen-Image is the trap: it exposes a true_cfg_scale and REQUIRES a negative_prompt argument, yet the Qwen2.5-VL encoder was not trained for negative conditioning, so the negative is weak-to-inert even at true_cfg_scale > 1.**

Qwen-Image's pipeline takes true_cfg_scale (default ~4.0) which does run a real two-pass CFG, and the negative_prompt parameter is mandatory for the pipeline to execute. But because the text encoder is a generative VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) rather than a contrastive CLIP, the model lacks the trained push-away behavior; practitioner testing across CFG 1.0-7.0 found essentially zero exclusion effect. The negative_prompt exists as a pipeline placeholder, not a working lever. Qwen ships positive_magic suffixes (', Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition.') and recommends specifying intent positively. So: structurally it has CFG, behaviorally it ignores negatives like a distilled model.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** On Qwen-Image, set negative_prompt to an empty string (' ') -- do not invest effort in it. Steer entirely via a detailed positive prompt plus the official positive_magic suffix. Treat its negatives as cosmetic, not functional.
- **Engine:** Qwen · **Base:** Qwen (Qwen-Image, Qwen2.5-VL encoder) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Grounded -- both sources verified. Official Qwen/Qwen-Image model card confirmed: pipeline uses true_cfg_scale=4.0, ships positive_magic suffixes (', Ultra HD, 4K, cinematic composition.'), and the card itself instructs negative_prompt = ' ' (empty string) 'if you do not have specific concept to remove' -- so the recommended-empty default is the OFFICIAL recommendation, not just community lore. PromptMaster blog verified: 2D grid test across CFG 1.0-7.0 trying to exclude 'child' showed 'zero effect across all CFG values'; negative_prompt is 'a placeholder for the CFG mechanism.' One precision note: the card does not literally print the word 'required' -- it includes negative_prompt in the call and defaults it to a single space; 'required argument' is fair in practice (the pipeline signature expects it) but is slightly stronger than the card's wording. Net: CONFIRMED; treat Qwen negatives as cosmetic and steer via positive + positive_magic.
- **Sources:** [Qwen/Qwen-Image model card (true_cfg_scale, required negative_prompt, positive_magic)](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image) (Qwen team, 2025) — Pipeline uses true_cfg_scale (~4.0) and requires a negative_prompt; ships positive_magic quality suffixes; recommends detailed positive prompting. ; [The Mystery of Qwen-Image's Ignored Negative Prompts](https://blog.promptmaster.pro/posts/qwen-image-negative-prompts/) (PromptMaster, 2025) — Qwen-Image was never trained to push away from negative content; testing CFG 1.0-7.0 showed zero exclusion effect; the negative_prompt is a required placeholder, not a functional lever.

### Even the SD1.5 negative embeddings are ANIME-trained on… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Even the SD1.5 negative embeddings are ANIME-trained on specific checkpoints and carry style baggage — they are not neutral 'quality boosters.'**

EasyNegative was trained WITH the Counterfeit anime checkpoint (8 vectors) and is intended for anime models (Anything v3, OrangeMix); its own README says 'effectiveness is not certain' on other models. ng_deepnegative and the bad-hands family are likewise anime-finetune artifacts. Because a TI embedding is a learned shortcut into ONE model's latent space, applying it elsewhere injects that model's aesthetic bias, not generic 'quality.' For a commercial 2.5D JRPG painterly/illustrative house style this is a style-contamination risk even where it loads, pulling toward generic anime rendering.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Do not treat negative embeddings as model-agnostic quality dials. If you ever use one (SD1.5 only), assume it injects the aesthetic of its training checkpoint (Counterfeit/anime) and A/B it against your locked style plate before trusting it. For a defined commercial art style, prefer an explicit, auditable text negative over an opaque embedding whose training data you can't inspect.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** SD1.5 anime finetunes only; folklore-misused as universal · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed from the EasyNegative dataset card (gsdf/EasyNegative README). It states 'This is a Negative Embedding trained with Counterfeit,' shows sample outputs from anime checkpoints (Counterfeit V2.0, AbyssOrangeMix2, Anything v4.0), and explicitly hedges cross-model transfer: 'It can be used with other models, but the effectiveness is not certain.' That directly supports 'anime-trained, carries the aesthetic of its training checkpoint, not a model-agnostic quality dial.' Minor over-reach: the comfyui-wiki source's specific '512-cropped anime data' detail is NOT stated on that page (it only classifies them as SD1.5 embeddings), so don't lean on the 512-crop specificity. The prompt_rule (don't treat negative embeddings as model-agnostic quality dials; A/B against your locked style plate; prefer auditable text negatives for a defined commercial style) is well-founded.
- **Sources:** [gsdf/EasyNegative dataset card (trained with Counterfeit; anime models; effectiveness uncertain elsewhere)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/gsdf/EasyNegative/blob/main/README.md) (gsdf, 2023) — EasyNegative is a negative embedding trained with Counterfeit, intended for anime models like Anything v3/OrangeMix; 'can be used with other models but effectiveness is not certain.' ; [Recommended Negative Embeddings for SD1.5 (anime-finetune lineage)](https://comfyui-wiki.com/en/resource/embedding-models) (DCAI / ComfyUI-Wiki, 2024) — EasyNegative/Deep-Negative/bad-hands family are SD1.5 anime-finetune embeddings trained on 512-cropped anime data.

### The giant 50-term 'worst quality, lowres, bad anatomy, bad… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**The giant 50-term 'worst quality, lowres, bad anatomy, bad hands, extra fingers, ...' block is largely FOLKLORE: most terms are inert and the long string actively DILUTES the few that matter.**

Two mechanisms work against the megablock. (1) Attention dilution: CLIP/T5 self-attention is softmax-normalized to sum to 1, so every token added spreads the fixed attention budget thinner — the 3 words that would have steered get drowned by 47 that don't. Research shows that even at zero scaling, a long negative sequence still 'distracts' image-token attention and can reduce quality. (2) A negative prompt cannot summon detail or anatomy the base model never learned; users testing 'bad hands/bad anatomy' negatives found basically zero measurable effect on hand quality — different seeds varied, but not better than empty-negative. The block is cargo-culted from anime-finetune defaults where a FEW quality tags genuinely fire (next finding), then copy-pasted everywhere it doesn't.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Cap negatives at 3-8 SPECIFIC, model-tested tokens, not 50. Build the list by ablation: generate with empty negative, then add ONE term at a time and keep only terms that visibly change the output for YOUR base+seed. Never paste a 50-word block — it is mostly placebo and measurably dilutes the working terms.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen (anywhere a real negative is honored) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The dilution mechanism is empirically grounded. VSF (arXiv:2508.10931, Section 3.3 'Attention Bias') states verbatim: 'even when the scaling factor alpha=0, including the negative prompt in the sequence still sometimes reduces image quality. This could be because the negative prompt distracts the image tokens attention from the image tokens or positive prompts.' That directly supports 'the long string actively DILUTES.' CAVEAT: the source's gloss about softmax normalization 'spreading attention thinner as tokens are added' is an extrapolation — VSF frames it as distraction, not as a formal softmax-normalization proof. Second source (HF stabilityai discussion #7857) could NOT be verified — it returns HTTP 401 (auth-gated), so the specific 'negatives can't fix hands across seeds' anecdote is UNVERIFIABLE as cited; however the broader point that negatives cannot synthesize anatomy the model never learned is consistent with the neutralization mechanism in Ban et al. The ablation-driven prompt_rule (build the list one term at a time, keep only what visibly changes YOUR base+seed) is sound engineering advice and the right corrective to the cargo-cult 50-word block.
- **Sources:** [VSF: Negative Guidance in Few-Step Models / attention-dilution analysis](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.10931) (VSF authors, 2025) — Even with zero scaling factor, including the negative prompt in the sequence reduces image quality because it distracts image-token attention; softmax normalization spreads attention thinner as tokens are added. arXiv:2508.10931 ; [stabilityai/stable-diffusion · Negative Prompts discussion + user hand-anatomy tests](https://huggingface.co/spaces/stabilityai/stable-diffusion/discussions/7857) (HF community, 2023) — Negatives targeting bad anatomy/bad hands showed basically zero effect on hand quality across seeds; negatives can't fix anatomy the model never learned.

### LICENSE / commercial-safety of these embeddings is UNVERIFIED · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**LICENSE / commercial-safety of these embeddings is UNVERIFIED — most carry 'license: other' or vague Civitai custom terms with no explicit commercial grant. This is a real liability for a commercial studio.**

The gsdf/EasyNegative dataset card states 'license: other' with NO explicit commercial-use grant; the HF mirror is sometimes tagged CDLA-Permissive-2.0, but the two disagree, so provenance is ambiguous. Civitai model pages use a patchwork of CreativeML OpenRAIL-M, custom restrictive flags, and unspecified terms; there is no reliable license filter, and a TI embedding's training-data provenance is opaque. For a commercial product, shipping art steered by an asset whose license is 'other/unverified' and whose training set is unknown is an avoidable legal exposure.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** For commercial JRPG art, do NOT ship outputs that depend on third-party negative embeddings unless you have a written, explicit commercial grant AND known training-data provenance. EasyNegative et al. fail both (license: 'other', no commercial grant, opaque data). Default to plain-text negatives, which carry zero licensing surface, on your CFG-honoring base models.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all third-party Civitai/HF negative embeddings · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources verified. The gsdf/EasyNegative dataset card lists the license field as 'other' with no explicit commercial-use grant. The Civitai discussion (orgs/civitai/discussions/267) confirms systemic license ambiguity: users state 'I can't even figure out which one I can generate images for commercial use and which I cannot,' creators use inconsistent/custom flags (some 'not even compatible with Open RAIL-M'), and there is no reliable license filter — commercial permission must be checked per-asset. For a commercial JRPG studio this is a genuine liability surface. The prompt_rule (don't ship outputs that depend on third-party negative embeddings without a written commercial grant plus known provenance; default to plain-text negatives which carry zero licensing surface) is correct and prudent.
- **Sources:** [gsdf/EasyNegative dataset card — license field](https://huggingface.co/datasets/gsdf/EasyNegative/blob/main/README.md) (gsdf, 2023) — License field reads 'other' with no explicit commercial-use grant stated. ; [Civitai licensing FAQ + 'we need a way to filter by license' discussion](https://github.com/orgs/civitai/discussions/267) (Civitai community, 2024) — Civitai assets use inconsistent/custom license flags with no reliable license filter; commercial permission must be checked per-asset and is frequently unspecified.

### A negative prompt is literally the CFG unconditional term… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**A negative prompt is literally the CFG unconditional term replaced by a conditioned term — it only exists because CFG subtracts it; with no real CFG it does nothing.**

CFG (Ho & Salimans 2022) computes the final noise as eps_uncond + scale*(eps_cond - eps_uncond).
