The community swap is: feed the negative prompt as the 'uncond' branch, so the model is pushed AWAY from eps_neg by exactly (scale-1). This is the entire mechanism. At CFG=1 the (eps_cond - eps_uncond) term vanishes and the negative branch is never evaluated — which is why FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, and SDXL-Turbo/Lightning (guidance-distilled, run at CFG≈1) silently discard any negative_prompt. The 'distilled/Flux guidance' slider is a baked-in scalar, NOT a second conditioning pass, so there is no eps_neg to subtract.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Only fill negative_prompt on un-distilled CFG models (base SDXL ~CFG 5-8, Chroma, Qwen-Image base). On FLUX-dev/schnell, Z-Image-Turbo, SDXL-Turbo/Lightning leave negative empty — every token you put there is dead weight that costs encode time and zero effect. If you genuinely need negative steering on FLUX, you must add a true-CFG node (real second pass), accepting ~2x compute.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all (mechanism); negatives ACTIVE on base-SDXL/Chroma/Qwen-Image-base, INERT on FLUX/Z-Image-Turbo/distilled-turbo · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Mechanism grounded. Ho & Salimans 2022 (arXiv:2207.12598) define CFG as combining conditional and unconditional score estimates (interpolation eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond)); the negative prompt is the well-documented community substitution of a conditioned term for the unconditional one (formula confirmed via the standard formulation and NAG arXiv:2505.21179: eps_hat = eps(c) + lambda*(eps(c) - eps(c-))). The FLUX-dev/schnell behavior is confirmed by the ComfyUI ecosystem: Flux-dev is distilled, you set KSampler CFG=1.0, and at CFG=1 the system skips the unconditional pass so plain negatives are ignored; real negative steering on FLUX requires a true-CFG / NAG node at ~2x compute. NOTE: the specific comfyui-wiki URL cited in the source list (flux-1-dev-t2i) does NOT itself state the CFG=1/negatives-ignored behavior — that page is install/hardware docs. The claim is true and well-sourced, just not at that exact URL; better citations are comfyanonymous.github.io/ComfyUI_examples/flux/ and the ComfyUI-NAG repo. The prompt_rule (only fill negatives on un-distilled CFG models) is correct.
- **Sources:** [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Ho, Salimans, 2022) — Defines CFG as interpolation eps_uncond + w*(eps_cond - eps_uncond); negative prompting is the community substitution of a conditioned term for the unconditional one. arXiv:2207.12598 ; [Flux.1 ComfyUI / Forge guidance behavior (CFG=1 skips uncond, negatives ignored)](https://comfyui-wiki.com/en/tutorial/advanced/image/flux/flux-1-dev-t2i) (ComfyUI-Wiki / lllyasviel Forge discussion, 2024) — Flux-dev/schnell are distilled; set CFG=1 and use no negative prompt — at CFG=1 the system skips unconditional conditioning and negatives are ignored.

### Negative TEXTUAL-INVERSION embeddings (EasyNegative,… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Negative TEXTUAL-INVERSION embeddings (EasyNegative, ng_deepnegative_v1_75t, bad-hands-5, badhandv4, FastNegativeV2) are SD1.5-only — they are dimensionally incompatible with SDXL and do nothing or corrupt on it.**

An SD1.5 TI embedding is a tensor of learned vectors in the 768-dim CLIP-ViT-L space. SDXL has TWO text encoders (CLIP-L 768 + OpenCLIP-bigG 1280, concatenated to 2048) and a native SDXL embedding stores a vector set for BOTH. A 768-only SD1.5 embedding has no 1280-dim half, so it cannot be injected into SDXL's bigG stream — loaders either error on the dimension mismatch or (in lenient UIs) load garbage that injects noise/off-style. Conversion tools only patch 'part of the text encoder' and are unreliable. None of FLUX/Chroma (T5-XXL) or Qwen/Z-Image (Qwen-VL/Qwen3) share CLIP's token-embedding space at all, so these embeddings are categorically inapplicable there.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Never load EasyNegative / ng_deepnegative / bad-hands-5 / badhandv4 / FastNegativeV2 on SDXL, FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image, or Z-Image — they were trained for SD1.5's single 768-dim CLIP and don't transfer. On SDXL use SDXL-NATIVE negative embeddings only (and verify they help via ablation). On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image there is no CLIP TI slot at all — use plain-text negatives (if CFG-honoring) instead.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP (and FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image — all incompatible); only valid on SD1.5 · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The dimensional incompatibility is real and well-grounded. The SDXL paper (arXiv:2307.01952) confirms SDXL concatenates CLIP-L (768-dim) and OpenCLIP-bigG (1280-dim) into a 2048-dim context, vs SD1.5's single 768-dim CLIP — an SD1.5 TI vector physically cannot populate both SDXL encoders. (The cited myByways URL does NOT state these dimensions — it only names the two encoders; the dimensional grounding comes from the SDXL paper itself, which is the better citation.) The Civitai incompatibility article confirms the behavioral outcome verbatim: SD1.5 embeds 'DO NOT WORK... only if they do work 10% of the time? They damage your output, are unpredictable' — though it attributes this to general architecture differences, not explicitly to dimension mismatch. comfyui-wiki lists EasyNegative/ng_deepnegative/badhandv4 under 'SD1.5 Version Embeddings.' The prompt_rule (never load SD1.5 negative embeds on SDXL/FLUX/Chroma/Qwen/Z-Image; use SDXL-native embeds only and ablate; on FLUX-family there is no CLIP TI slot so use text negatives) is correct.
- **Sources:** [Two Text Prompts (Text Encoders) in SDXL 1.0 — CLIP-L 768 + bigG 1280 → 2048](https://mybyways.com/blog/two-text-prompts-text-encoders-in-sdxl-1-0) (myByways, 2023) — SDXL concatenates [B,77,768] from CLIP-L and [B,77,1280] from OpenCLIP-bigG into [B,77,2048]; an embedding must supply vectors for both encoders' dimensions. ; [The Incompatibility of SD 1.5 Embeds with SDXL/PDXL](https://civitai.com/articles/4859/the-incompatibility-of-sd-15-embeds-with-sdxlpdxl) (Civitai author, 2024) — SD1.5 embeds 'DO NOT WORK' on SDXL — only ~10% of the time and then they damage output; conversions only tackle part of the text encoder.

### Negatives share the SAME 77-token CLIP budget as the positive · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Negatives share the SAME 77-token CLIP budget as the positive — a bloated negative truncates silently and high CFG turns leftover negatives into burn.**

Each CLIP encoder caps at 77 tokens (75 usable + BOS/EOS); the negative prompt gets its OWN 77-token window but diffusers/most UIs TRUNCATE silently past it — so a 50-term megablock that overflows means later terms (often the 'important' ones a user appended) are dropped without warning. Separately, piling on negatives invites cranking CFG to 'make them bite,' but high CFG on SDXL/SD-lineage causes oversaturation/burnout — the exact failure Lin et al. 2023 (rescale-CFG, arXiv:2305.08891) document and fix. So 'long negative + high CFG' is a double cargo-cult: truncation loses terms AND the high CFG degrades the image. (T5 in Chroma/FLUX allows far longer context, so the 77-token truncation specifically is a CLIP-encoder problem.)  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Keep the negative well under 75 tokens on any CLIP model (SDXL) — assume silent truncation past it, so a 50-word block may be dropping your real terms. Don't raise CFG to compensate for a weak negative; if SDXL output looks oversaturated/burnt, apply CFG-rescale (Lin et al. 2023) rather than fighting it with more negatives.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5 · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP (77-token + burn); Chroma-T5/FLUX have longer context (truncation less of an issue, but FLUX still ignores negatives) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both halves grounded. The 77-token CLIP limit (75 usable + BOS/EOS) is real and confirmed by diffusers issue #2136 ('CLIP has a 77 token limit'); negatives are tokenized through the same encoder as positives, so they share/compete for the budget and are truncated past 77 by default in vanilla diffusers. CAVEAT: issue #2136 frames truncation implicitly (it is a feature-request to OVERCOME the limit, describing the A1111 75-token-chunking workaround) rather than stating 'we silently truncate negatives by default' in those words — the truncation default is real but the citation is framed as a request, so it is supporting-not-authoritative. NOTE many UIs (A1111, ComfyUI) chunk beyond 77 rather than hard-truncate, so 'silently truncates' is implementation-dependent — true for raw diffusers, softened in chunking UIs. The CFG-rescale half is solidly confirmed: Lin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2305.08891, 'Common Diffusion Noise Schedules and Sample Steps are Flawed') finds high CFG causes over-exposure and proposes rescaling CFG to prevent it. The prompt_rule (keep negatives well under 75 tokens; don't raise CFG to compensate; apply CFG-rescale rather than fighting burn with more negatives) is correct.
- **Sources:** [Overcoming the 77-token limit in diffusers (CLIP context length, silent truncation)](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/2136) (huggingface/diffusers, 2023) — CLIP context length is 77 tokens (75 usable + BOS/EOS); diffusers truncates tokenized prompts beyond 77 by default, for negative as well as positive. ; [Common Diffusion Noise Schedules and Sample Steps are Flawed (CFG-rescale)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.08891) (Lin, Liu, Li, Yang (Lin et al.), 2023) — High classifier-free guidance causes over-exposure/burnout; the paper proposes rescaling CFG to prevent oversaturation. arXiv:2305.08891

### Quality-WORD negatives ('worst quality, low quality,… · `recommended` · community-claim

**Quality-WORD negatives ('worst quality, low quality, lowres, normal quality') are a booru-finetune artifact and are PLACEBO on non-anime / photoreal / painterly bases.**

Tags like 'masterpiece / worst quality / low quality' fire on anime models because Danbooru/booru training data was literally tagged with those quality buckets — the model learned a real association between the token and image quality. Photoreal and many painterly/illustrative bases were NOT trained on that tag vocabulary, so the token has no learned referent and steering is near-zero ('placebo' per practitioner consensus). For a 2.5D JRPG built on SDXL photoreal/painterly checkpoints (not a booru finetune), copying anime quality-negatives in adds dilution (see finding 2) for no benefit.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Only use 'worst quality/low quality/masterpiece'-style quality tags if your specific checkpoint is a booru/anime finetune that was TRAINED on them — verify by ablation. On photoreal or painterly JRPG bases, drop quality-word negatives entirely and negate concrete visual artifacts you actually see (e.g. 'jpeg artifacts', 'oversharpened halos') instead.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP (and any base): effective only on booru/anime finetunes; placebo on photoreal/painterly bases · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CORRECTED: HALF-CONFIRMED, half-unsupported as cited — this is the weakest finding in the set. The POSITIVE half is solid: both sources confirm quality/meta tags work on booru/Danbooru-trained models BECAUSE the training data was bucketed/tagged by community quality ratings (Tech Tactician: images 'categorized into buckets based on their community ratings... prefix your prompt with specific score/quality triggers'; Civitai 25464: tags work because of 'the composition of tagged training data'). But the load-bearing NEGATIVE half — that these tags are 'PLACEBO on non-anime / photoreal / painterly bases' — is NOT stated by either cited source. Tech Tactician makes no comparative claim about realistic models, and Civitai 25464 explicitly does NOT argue that non-booru models fail to recognize the tags. The 'placebo on realistic' conclusion is a plausible INFERENCE from the training-data mechanism, not a sourced empirical finding. Correction: keep the ablation-first prompt_rule (verify on YOUR checkpoint; negate concrete visual artifacts you actually see), but downgrade the confidence — frame the realistic-model placebo as 'likely inert, verify by ablation,' NOT as an established fact. Note also the over-broad 'painterly' lumping: a painterly checkpoint could be a booru-anime finetune that DOES respond. The verdict on the rule (ablate, don't cargo-cult quality words) stands; the verdict on the stated empirical claim is CORRECTED for citation overreach.
- **Sources:** [Booru-Style Tagging with SDXL Anime Models — quality tags work on anime, are placebo on realistic](https://techtactician.com/booru-style-tagging-sdxl-anime-prompts-guide/) (Tech Tactician, 2026) — Quality tag weighting works for anime models because booru training data was tagged that way; on many realistic models the same quality tags are placebo. ; [Common style/quality tags recognized by Illustrious & Danbooru-based models](https://civitai.com/articles/25464/common-style-tags-recognized-by-illustrious-and-other-danbooru-based-models) (Civitai author, 2025) — Quality/meta tags are recognized because high-quality training images were tagged with them; models not trained on that vocabulary do not respond.

### Stacking negatives can BACKFIRE and generate the very thing… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Stacking negatives can BACKFIRE and generate the very thing you negated — the 'Reverse Activation' phenomenon, strongest with early/high-strength negatives.**

ECCV 2024 (arXiv:2406.02965) is the load-bearing empirical study. Negatives work by Deletion-through-Neutralization: the negative branch must first generate the target object at the same location so the subtraction cancels it. This has a DELAYED EFFECT — peak removal for nouns is around step 5, adjectives plateau ~step 10. If a negative is applied too early (steps 1-4) two effects (Inducing + Momentum, ~99.5% step-to-step noise correlation) can lock generative momentum TOWARD the negated object, materializing it instead of removing it. So a heavy, early, high-CFG negative is not 'more safety' — it raises the odds of summoning the artifact.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Treat negatives as scalpels, not insurance. Keep CFG moderate (SDXL ~5-7), keep the negative SHORT, and don't assume 'more negative = safer' — past a point it inverts. If a specific artifact KEEPS appearing despite being negated, that's Reverse Activation: remove that exact term from the negative (or schedule it to start ~step 5+) rather than strengthening it.
- **Engine:** CLIP/T5/Qwen · **Base:** SDXL-CLIP, Chroma-T5, Qwen (CFG-honoring models) · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Fully grounded in Ban et al., 'Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?' (ECCV 2024, arXiv:2406.02965). Confirmed verbatim from the paper HTML: Reverse Activation — 'introducing a negative prompt in the early stages of diffusion paradoxically results in the generation of the specified object in the initial generation stage'; Inducing Effect — 'the negative prompt triggers the positive noise in a direction that represents the context of the negative prompt'; Momentum Effect — estimated noises keep the same direction, with 'a strikingly high correlation up to 99.5% in the first 25 steps'; noun-based negatives 'peak at the 5th step.' Every specific number and mechanism in the claim checks out. The prompt_rule (treat negatives as scalpels, keep CFG moderate/SDXL ~5-7, and if an artifact keeps appearing despite negation, remove it or schedule it to start ~step 5 rather than strengthening) is a correct operationalization of the paper's delayed-neutralization-plus-Reverse-Activation finding.
- **Sources:** [Understanding the Impact of Negative Prompts: When and How Do They Take Effect?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02965) (Ban et al. (ECCV 2024), 2024) — Negatives act via delayed neutralization (noun removal peaks ~step 5); early/high-strength negatives can trigger Reverse Activation via Inducing + Momentum effects (99.5% step-to-step noise correlation), generating the negated concept. arXiv:2406.02965

## Seed & sampling

### To A/B a prompt change cleanly, LOCK the seed and change… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**To A/B a prompt change cleanly, LOCK the seed and change exactly ONE token. With z_T held fixed, every pixel difference is attributable to that one edit.**

Because the pipeline is deterministic given (seed, prompt, sampler, steps, CFG, resolution, model), fixing the seed and changing a single token isolates the causal effect of that token: composition stays roughly anchored by the shared z_T, so the delta you see is the edit's contribution, not noise. The official HuggingFace Diffusers guide builds its prompt-engineering workflow on exactly this — generate a batch, pick one, then 'keep the first seed so that the images are similar to the first image' while improving the prompt. This is how you learn what a token actually does in YOUR model before committing it to a production prompt. It also exposes silently-ignored tokens: if a one-token change under a locked seed produces zero visible difference, that token is being dropped by the encoder (a prompt-fixable signal, not a seed one).  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** When testing a prompt edit, freeze the seed (and sampler/steps/CFG/resolution/model) and change ONE token or phrase per generation — never the seed and the prompt together. Read the delta against the locked baseline. If the locked-seed edit moves the image -> the token is active, keep iterating on this seed. If it moves nothing -> the encoder is ignoring it; reword, reorder, or reweight rather than re-rolling.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Directly supported by the official Hugging Face Diffusers doc (Reusing seeds for fast prompt engineering, v0.13.0): pass a fixed torch.Generator().manual_seed across runs and vary only the prompt so 'the images are similar to the first image,' isolating the edit. Minor refinement to the prompt_rule: locking the seed isolates the change well in practice but is NOT a perfect ceteris-paribus experiment — a single-token edit perturbs the cross-attention map globally, so non-trivial layout shifts can still occur even with z_T frozen (especially on CLIP-based SDXL). The 'every pixel difference is attributable to that one edit' phrasing is an idealization; the technique is correct and is the right way to A/B, just don't expect surgical pixel-locality.
- **Sources:** [Re-using seeds for fast prompt engineering (Diffusers docs)](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/v0.13.0/en/using-diffusers/reusing_seeds) (Hugging Face, 2023) — Pass a fixed torch.Generator().manual_seed(0) across generations and vary only the prompt so 'the images are similar to the first image' — isolating the prompt edit's effect from noise.

### Before rewriting a prompt for a 'missing element', check CFG · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Before rewriting a prompt for a 'missing element', check CFG — under-guidance reads as a prompt miss but is fixed by the guidance scale, not re-wording. Over-guidance burns quality and faces.**

Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, arXiv 2207.12598) sets how hard the model is pushed toward the conditioning by extrapolating between the conditional and unconditional predictions at each step. Too low, and requested elements get under-expressed or dropped — which mimics a prompt failure even though the prompt is fine. Too high, and you get oversaturation, mode collapse, and degraded/melted faces — which mimics a seed/instance failure even though the prompt is fine. CFG is therefore a third axis that masquerades as both: a missing-element symptom is sometimes a guidance floor problem, and an ugly-instance symptom is sometimes a guidance ceiling problem. It must be ruled out before you spend edits on either the seed or the prompt wording. Note FLUX-family models use a distilled/embedded guidance that behaves differently from SDXL's CFG scale — the principle holds, the dial doesn't transfer.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** When an element is faint or dropped, before rewording: nudge CFG UP a notch (locked seed, locked prompt) and see if it appears — under-guidance, not a prompt miss. When faces/skin look fried or oversaturated, nudge CFG DOWN before blaming the seed — over-guidance, not an unlucky instance. Only after CFG is dialed correctly do you decide seed vs prompt. (FLUX/Chroma: use their guidance-embedding dial, not SDXL CFG values.)

- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Ho & Salimans 2022 (Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance, arXiv:2207.12598) confirms the mechanism: combining conditional and unconditional score estimates trades off sample quality against diversity; higher guidance increases prompt adherence at the cost of fidelity/diversity. This grounds 'CFG up -> element appears (under-guidance), CFG down -> faces stop frying (over-guidance).' The McCormick blog (popular explainer, not primary) restates this correctly. The prompt_rule's instruction to dial CFG before deciding seed-vs-prompt is operationally sound. One correction to the FLUX aside: FLUX dev uses a distilled GUIDANCE-EMBEDDING scalar (not true CFG, since dev runs CFG=1 with the guidance baked into a conditioning embedding), so 'use their guidance dial, not SDXL CFG values' is right — but note that on guidance-distilled models pushing this dial does not behave like classic CFG extrapolation and over-cranking degrades differently. Claim CONFIRMED; treat the FLUX/Chroma guidance dial as a different knob, not a renamed CFG.

### The diagnostic: RIGHT KIND of thing, unlucky INSTANCE ->… · `recommended` · community-claim

**The diagnostic: RIGHT KIND of thing, unlucky INSTANCE -> re-roll the seed. WRONG KIND of thing -> fix the prompt. Re-rolling a prompt miss only hands you N more of the same miss.**

Empirically, similar prompts initialized from the same noise produce visually similar low-level structure (pose, colour gradients, layout); the prompt guides semantic content but the seed anchors the structural scaffold. So if the model is producing the right category of output and the only problem is THIS instance (an awkward hand, an on-spec but unappealing face, a slightly stiff pose, a minor glitch), the conditioning is doing its job — you just landed on a poor z_T, and a different z_T will land elsewhere. But if a requested element is absent or wrong (missing prop, wrong outfit, ignored 'scar over left eye', generic merc when you asked for a specific silhouette, a non-magnetic character), that absence lives in the conditioning, and every z_T denoised under the same instruction reproduces the same absence. Re-rolling explores the distribution the prompt defines; it cannot add a mode the prompt never requested.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** Apply the one-question test: 'If I generated 10 more seeds of THIS exact prompt, would the defect plausibly disappear on some of them?' If yes (bad hand, awkward pose, unappealing-but-on-spec face) -> seed problem, batch it. If no — the miss would recur every time (element absent, attribute ignored, wrong style, generic) -> prompt problem, stop generating and rewrite. The 'generic nobody' failure is a NO: every re-roll returns another generic nobody, because nothing in the prompt makes the character specific.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The diagnostic is sound and the operational logic is correct: a content miss (absent element, ignored attribute, wrong style, 'generic nobody') recurs across seeds because nothing in the conditioning makes it appear, while an instance defect (bad hand, awkward pose) is seed-distributed and batchable. SOURCING CORRECTION: the second cited source — AUTOMATIC1111 Discussion #6217 ('asked for a carpet, got a dog, re-seeding doesn't fix it') — does NOT contain that content. #6217 is about a Hires Fix algorithm regression (commit 4dbde22 producing body horrors after the upscaler was rewritten), not prompt-interpretation vs noise-instance. The 'carpet/dog' anecdote is not in that thread. The getimg.ai guide also does not explicitly state the composition-vs-content split. The CLAIM stands on its own logic and is corroborated indirectly (a content the conditioning never requests cannot appear by chance), but the specific citation is mischaracterized — treat finding 2's sourcing as folklore-grade, claim itself CONFIRMED on first principles + the LDM conditioning mechanism.

Same-seed/different-prompt is not a reliable way to change subject because the prompt drives semantics. ; [AUTOMATIC1111 webui Discussion #6217 / #7578 — same seed, prompt interpretation, and quality](https://github.com/AUTOMATIC1111/stable-diffusion-webui/discussions/6217) (AUTOMATIC1111 community, 2023) — When the model returns the wrong content (asked for a carpet, got a dog), re-seeding does not fix it; the issue is prompt/model interpretation, not the noise instance.

### ❌ DON'T — magic seeds' that fix a bad prompt do not exist. 'Golden'… · `avoid` · community-claim

**FOLKLORE ZONE: 'magic seeds' that fix a bad prompt do not exist. 'Golden' seeds raise AVERAGE aesthetic quality a little — they cannot add a missing element a prompt never requested.**

The research that sounds like it supports magic seeds actually bounds them. 'Good Seed Makes a Good Crop' (arXiv 2405.14828) finds ~65-67 'golden' seeds whose aggregate FID is better (best 21.60 vs worst 31.97) and whose ranking partially generalizes across prompts — but that is a small statistical bump in overall image quality (sharpness, fewer artifacts), NOT a fix for content. No seed makes the model render an object you didn't ask for, bind an attribute the encoder dropped, or make a generic character magnetic. Seeds are also NOT portable across models or even across model versions/schedulers — the same number indexes a different noise field per RNG/model, so a seed someone shares as 'amazing' carries no guarantee in your stack. Treat any claim of a seed that 'fixes prompts' or 'works everywhere' as folklore.  [grounding: folklore-DEBUNKED]

- **For the pipeline:** Never hunt for a magic seed to fix a content miss — it is a category error and wastes render time (this is exactly the 'generic nobody' trap). Do not trust shared/borrowed 'great seeds' across models, versions, or schedulers; re-derive your own. The only legitimate seed search is batching for the best COMPOSITION under an already-correct prompt — and even then the quality gain is marginal vs fixing the prompt.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** anti-pattern
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The folklore-debunked framing is correct and well-sourced. 'Good Seed Makes a Good Crop' (arXiv:2405.14828) confirms the FID figures (golden 21.60 vs inferior 31.97) and shows seeds affect interpretable VISUAL dimensions — object location, size, depth, grayscale tendency, sky regions — i.e. an aesthetic/compositional-prior effect, NOT a content/prompt-adherence fix. So no seed adds an element the prompt never requested. The seed-transfer half is independently confirmed: per multiple community sources, the same seed across different model versions, schedulers, or resolutions does NOT reproduce the same image, and CLIP guidance can weaken the seed's influence — a seed is a starting point for one model's RNG state, not a portable magic number. Two minor sourcing notes: (a) the Artlist blog cited returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, but its claim is corroborated by AUTOMATIC1111 Discussion #7578 and unimatrixz troubleshooting writeups; (b) the finding's own gloss that golden seeds 'partially generalize across prompts' is NOT clearly claimed by the 2405.14828 abstract (which emphasizes per-prompt seed mining) — drop that sub-claim. Core verdict: the magic-seed and seed-transfer beliefs are correctly DEBUNKED.

### Once the prompt is RIGHT, run a BATCH of N seeds to explore… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Once the prompt is RIGHT, run a BATCH of N seeds to explore composition — that's the legitimate, productive use of re-rolling.**

After the conditioning reliably produces the right kind of output, the remaining variation (pose, framing, face, hand layout) is pure z_T lottery, and the correct move is to sample that lottery in bulk rather than one-at-a-time. The Diffusers workflow is explicitly two-phase: first generate a batch with a LIST of generators (one seed each), then lock onto the winner. In production this is throughput discipline: a batch of 8-16 seeds on a fixed good prompt surfaces the best instance far faster than serial single re-rolls, and because each image is tied to exactly one reproducible seed, the winner is re-summonable for downstream variation (expressions, angles) by holding its seed and editing the prompt.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** When the defect is composition (not content), do NOT re-roll one seed at a time — fire a batch of 8-16 seeds against the FROZEN prompt in a single run, with each image bound to its own logged seed. Pick the winner by eye, record its seed number, then iterate. Batching is the seed-side tool; reserve serial single re-rolls for nothing.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Both sources support this. Hugging Face Diffusers doc confirms the canonical pattern verbatim: 'generate a batch of images, select one image and improve it' by passing a list of generators each tied to one seed (num_images_per_prompt) so 'every single generated image in the batch is tied exactly to one seed.' The 'All Seeds Are Not Equal' paper (arXiv:2411.18810) confirms 'different initial random seeds tend to guide the model to place objects in distinct image areas... associated with the seed,' and sampling across seeds is how you find layouts that place requested elements correctly (numerical composition +29.3%, spatial +60.7% for SD after fine-tuning on mined good-seed images). Batching is the correct seed-side tool.
- **Sources:** [Re-using seeds for fast prompt engineering (Diffusers docs)](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/v0.13.0/en/using-diffusers/reusing_seeds) (Hugging Face, 2023) — Generate a batch by passing a list of generators each tied to one seed (num_images_per_prompt), select one, then refine — the canonical explore-then-lock loop. ; [All Seeds Are Not Equal: Enhancing Compositional Text-to-Image Generation with Reliable Random Seeds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18810) (Anonymous (arXiv 2411.18810), 2024) — Each seed produces distinct object-placement layouts; sampling across seeds is how you find the composition that places all requested elements correctly. arXiv:2411.18810

### The production loop is · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**The production loop is: find a GOOD seed first, then iterate the PROMPT on it. Lock the winning z_T and refine content against a stable scaffold.**

Because a fixed seed preserves low-level structure (pose, layout, colour) across prompt edits while the prompt re-steers semantics, the efficient pipeline inverts naive trial-and-error: you batch-explore to find a z_T whose composition you love, lock it, then do all subsequent content refinement (style adjectives, attribute fixes, expression, costume detail) on that one seed. Each edit moves only what the token controls; the framing you liked stays put. This is also how you build a character SHEET — lock the hero's hero-seed, then vary the prompt for expressions and angles to keep the silhouette consistent. The trap is doing it backwards (rerolling seeds while ALSO editing the prompt), which confounds the two effects and teaches you nothing.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** Two-phase always: (1) EXPLORE — batch seeds on a fixed prompt, pick the composition winner, write down its seed. (2) REFINE — lock that seed and change only the prompt, one lever at a time. Never re-roll the seed and edit the prompt in the same step. When you have your hero pose, keep that seed to spin off expression/angle variants on a consistent silhouette.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The two-phase explore-then-lock loop is directly documented by Hugging Face Diffusers (select an image from a seeded batch, keep its seed while improving the prompt so refined images stay similar to the chosen one). The getimg.ai guide independently confirms the refine half: with seed 438233955 locked, 'modifying just one word that defines emotion changes her facial expression while maintaining the other visual features like hair, clothes, and background' (smiling/laughing/sad/angry variants). IMPORTANT GUARD on the final sentence ('keep that seed to spin off expression/angle variants on a consistent silhouette'): a fixed seed gives APPROXIMATE consistency for SMALL prompt deltas (an expression word), not reliable character consistency for large changes like a new camera angle or full pose. A locked seed is NOT a character-consistency mechanism — large prompt edits drift the identity, and angle changes especially break it. For genuine cross-pose character consistency you need IP-Adapter / reference / LoRA / fine-tune, not seed reuse. Claim CONFIRMED for the small-delta refine loop; the angle-variant aside overstates what a fixed seed buys you.
- **Sources:** [Re-using seeds for fast prompt engineering (Diffusers docs)](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/v0.13.0/en/using-diffusers/reusing_seeds) (Hugging Face, 2023) — Select an image from a seeded batch, then keep its seed while improving the prompt so the refined images stay similar to the chosen one. ; [Guide to using Seed in Stable Diffusion](https://getimg.ai/guides/guide-to-seed-parameter-in-stable-diffusion) (getimg.ai, 2024) — Lock the seed and modify a single descriptive word (e.g. an emotion) to change one feature while preserving hair, clothes, and background from the same composition.

### The seed is the initial noise latent (z_T) · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**The seed is the initial noise latent (z_T); the prompt is the cross-attention conditioning. They control different things — the seed seeds the COMPOSITION, the prompt steers the CONTENT.**

In latent diffusion (Rombach 2022), generation starts from a random Gaussian latent z_T selected by the seed, and a U-Net iteratively denoises it toward z_0; the text prompt enters only as a conditioning signal through cross-attention layers at each denoising step (Ho 2020 DDPM is the underlying reverse process). The denoising trajectory is therefore a function of BOTH inputs: the same seed + same prompt is fully deterministic (identical pixels), so any change in output is attributable to exactly one of the two knobs. This is the mechanical basis for the whole re-roll-vs-rewrite decision: re-rolling swaps z_T (a new structural starting point, same semantic instruction); rewriting changes the instruction (same or new starting point). Confusing the two is the root error behind the 'generic slouching nobody' incident — re-rendering and tweaking tonemaps changes neither z_T's semantics nor the conditioning in a way that fixes a content miss.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** Before touching anything on a bad result, name the defect as either COMPOSITION (a property of this z_T: pose, framing, object placement, hand layout, this particular face) or CONTENT (a property of the instruction: a missing element, wrong style, ignored attribute, generic-when-asked-specific). Composition defect -> re-roll the seed. Content defect -> rewrite the prompt. Never tweak render/tonemap/lighting to fix either — those touch neither z_T nor the conditioning.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: The two architectural facts are solidly sourced. Rombach et al. 2022 (LDM/Stable Diffusion, arXiv:2112.10752) is confirmed verbatim: the model denoises a latent and 'By introducing cross-attention layers into the model architecture, we turn diffusion models into powerful and flexible generators for general conditioning inputs such as text.' Ho et al. 2020 (DDPM, arXiv:2006.11239) defines the reverse process from Gaussian noise x_T to x_0 (Algorithm 2 starts x_T ~ N(0,I)) — this is foundational and universally accepted, though the arXiv abstract page is too thin to quote the algorithm and the PDF returned as binary; verdict rests on the well-established result, not a fresh quote. CAVEAT on the prompt_rule, not the citations: the clean 'seed = composition / prompt = content' split is a useful heuristic, not a strict separation. z_T and the conditioning interact through every cross-attention layer at every step — a new seed changes content-relevant details (which face, which object instance), and the prompt influences global layout. The diagnostic in finding 1 is directionally right; do not treat the seed/prompt boundary as a clean partition of pixels.
- **Sources:** [High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752) (Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, Ommer, 2022) — LDM denoises a random latent z_T to z_0; text conditioning is injected via cross-attention layers, separating the stochastic structural seed from the semantic instruction. arXiv:2112.10752 ; [Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239) (Ho, Jain, Abbeel, 2020) — Defines the reverse denoising process from Gaussian noise x_T to x_0; the initial noise sample (the seed) is the starting point of a deterministic-given-noise trajectory. arXiv:2006.11239

### Whether a defect is even seed-fixable depends on the text… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**Whether a defect is even seed-fixable depends on the text encoder. CLIP (SDXL) drops attributes and mis-binds adjectives as a STRUCTURAL limit — re-rolling never fixes a CLIP binding miss; switch tactics (or model) instead.**

SDXL conditions on CLIP encoders that behave bag-of-words cross-modally: with multiple objects, an adjective routinely binds to the wrong noun or is ignored ('red sword, blue cloak' yields a blue sword), and negation/counting fail. This is an encoder property, invariant to the seed — so on SDXL, an attribute-binding or missing-element miss is firmly prompt-side and often needs structural fixes (split into regional prompts, reduce competing attributes, reorder, reweight) rather than re-wording alone. T5/LLM-conditioned models (FLUX, Chroma, Qwen-Image) have markedly stronger natural-language adherence and longer token budgets, so a miss that is hopeless to seed-fix on SDXL may simply be a wording fix there. The seed-vs-prompt decision is the same everywhere; the PROMPT ceiling — how much the prompt can be trusted to land — moves with the encoder.  [grounding: empirical-paper]

- **For the pipeline:** On SDXL/CLIP: treat any attribute-binding or missing-element miss as encoder-structural — do NOT re-roll and do NOT just re-word; reduce competing attributes, use regional/split prompting, reorder so the key noun+adjective lead, and reweight. On FLUX/Chroma/Qwen: a content miss is more often a plain wording/specificity fix — rewrite naturally and verify with a locked-seed A/B before batching.
- **Engine:** CLIP · **Base:** SDXL · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CORRECTED: The operational conclusion is right (re-rolling the noise does not fix an attribute-binding miss — that is a conditioning-side problem, not a z_T problem), but the CLIP source is MISCHARACTERIZED. arXiv:2502.03566 ('CLIP Behaves like a Bag-of-Words Model Cross-modally but not Uni-modally') argues the OPPOSITE of a 'structural encoder limit': it finds 'attribute-object bindings are already encoded within CLIP's text and image embeddings' and 'CLIP does not lack binding information' uni-modally — the weakness is in CROSS-MODAL ALIGNMENT, and it is fixable with 'a simple linear transformation to text embeddings.' So binding failure is an alignment artifact, not an immutable encoder ceiling. Correction to the claim: re-rolling the seed indeed won't fix a binding miss (CONFIRMED operationally), but calling it a hard structural limit overstates the cited paper; the better SDXL tactics (reduce competing attributes, regional/split prompting, reorder so key noun+adjective lead, reweight) are correct mitigations. The FLUX/T5 half is community-sourced (pxz.ai, opinion/marketing-grade, not primary) — directionally accepted (T5 with longer context generally improves complex-prompt adherence vs dual CLIP) but not rigorously established by that source. Net: keep the prompt_rule; fix the rationale from 'structural encoder limit' to 'cross-modal alignment weakness, noise-invariant either way.'
- **Sources:** [CLIP Behaves like a Bag-of-Words Model Cross-modally but not Uni-modally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03566) ((arXiv 2502.03566), 2025) — CLIP's cross-modal bag-of-words behavior causes attribute mis-binding and ignored adjectives — a structural encoder limit, not a noise-instance effect. arXiv:2502.03566 ; [Flux vs SDXL 2026: Quality, Speed & Hardware Compared](https://pxz.ai/blog/flux-vs-sdxl) (pxz.ai, 2026) — FLUX's T5 encoder (up to 512 tokens) gives stronger complex-prompt adherence than SDXL's dual CLIP encoders, raising the prompt-trust ceiling.

### Ancestral and SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM2 a, DPM++ 2S a,… · `recommended` · community-claim

**Ancestral and SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM2 a, DPM++ 2S a, DPM++ SDE, DPM++ 2M SDE) inject FRESH random noise every step, so they are markedly less seed-stable and never fully converge; deterministic samplers (DDIM, Euler, Heun, DPM++ 2M, LMS) reproduce exactly from the same seed.**

Ancestral/SDE variants 'add, in each new step, random variables' — re-adding noise after each denoise step. Because there is always new noise to remove, they never converge, and reproduction can fail even with the identical seed and parameters (different sampler implementations/versions diverge). Deterministic samplers follow a fixed ODE trajectory and give 'the exact same image every single time' for a given seed+settings. This is why an operator chasing reproducibility or a stable base image gets burned by Euler a.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** For the production/consistency pipeline (where you re-render, upscale, or seed-sweep and need stability), use a DETERMINISTIC sampler — DDIM, Euler, Heun, DPM++ 2M / 2M Karras. Reserve ancestral/SDE samplers (Euler a, DPM++ SDE) for exploration/variety where you WANT each step to add character. If a seed 'won't reproduce' despite identical settings, check the sampler first — an ancestral/SDE sampler is the usual culprit, not a bad seed.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** sampler-specific · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed against the cited Felix Sanz 'Complete guide to samplers' article: ancestral samplers 'add, in each new step, random variables obtained from previous steps' and 'never converge because of the random noise added in each step'; and under Reproducibility it states that if you cannot reproduce an image despite the same seed and parameters, 'it may be because you are using an ancestral sampler.' The guide's classification matches the claim: ancestral/SDE = Euler a, DPM2 a, DPM++ 2S a, DPM++ SDE, DPM++ 2M SDE Karras (non-convergent); deterministic = DDIM, Euler, Heun, LMS, DPM2, DPM++ 2M, UniPC (convergent). One precision note: the claim lists 'DPM++ 2M SDE' generically as ancestral -- correct (any SDE variant injects per-step noise); and 'DPM2 a' (the ancestral variant) is ancestral while plain 'DPM2' is deterministic, which the source corroborates. The second source (stable-diffusion-art/samplers) 403'd and could not be fetched, but the primary source fully establishes the claim. Practice (deterministic samplers for re-render/upscale/seed-sweep stability; check the sampler first when a seed won't reproduce) is sound. CONFIRMED.
- **Sources:** [Complete guide to samplers in Stable Diffusion](https://www.felixsanz.dev/articles/complete-guide-to-samplers-in-stable-diffusion) (Félix Sanz, 2023) — Ancestral samplers add random noise each step and never converge; if you cannot reproduce an image with the same seed and parameters it may be because you used an ancestral sampler. Deterministic samplers (DDIM, Euler, DPM++ 2M) converge and reproduce. ; [Stable Diffusion Samplers: A Comprehensive Guide](https://stable-diffusion-art.com/samplers/) (Andrew (stable-diffusion-art), 2024) — DDIM/deterministic samplers give repeatable results for a fixed seed; ancestral samplers (Euler a) inject randomness each step and are less seed-stable, e.g. less effective with seed resize.

### CFG scale — not the seed — is the dial for 'follow the… · `recommended` · reproduced-from-source

**CFG scale — not the seed — is the dial for 'follow the prompt harder'. When a character is generic/off-identity, raising CFG (within a sane band) increases prompt adherence; re-rolling the seed cannot.**

Classifier-free guidance combines the conditional and unconditional model predictions with a guidance weight: higher CFG pushes the output toward the prompt, lower CFG makes it more diverse/random. The seed is orthogonal to this — it picks the noise, CFG picks how hard the noise is bent toward the prompt. A guidance range around 4-10 (defaults ~7-8 for many SDXL-era models) balances adherence vs diversity; FLUX/distilled and Qwen/Z-Image families use their own much lower 'distilled guidance' scales, so the band is model-specific.  [grounding: official-docs]

- **For the pipeline:** When the SUBJECT is under-rendered or generic, before re-rolling: (1) strengthen the identity tokens in the prompt, then (2) nudge CFG up toward the upper end of the model's band (SDXL ~7-9). If raising CFG makes it fried/over-saturated instead of more on-prompt, the prompt itself lacks the identity content — fix the prompt. Use the model-appropriate CFG band (do not apply SDXL's CFG 7 to FLUX/Qwen/Z-Image distilled-guidance, which want much lower values). The seed is the LAST lever, only after subject and CFG are right.
- **Engine:** all · **Base:** all · **Kind:** technique
- **Verify:** CONFIRMED: Confirmed against the cited theory sources. Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho/Salimans 2022, arxiv 2207.12598) confirms the guidance scale interpolates conditional vs unconditional score estimates to trade sample quality (fidelity/adherence) against diversity -- i.e. higher CFG = stronger prompt adherence, which the seed cannot provide. LDM (Rombach et al. 2022, arxiv 2112.10752) confirms text conditioning enters via cross-attention and steers denoising independently of the initial noise. So CFG is mechanistically the prompt-adherence dial and the seed is not. The practical caveats are correct and important: raising CFG only helps if the prompt CONTAINS the identity content (otherwise it over-saturates/fries), and the named CFG bands are model-dependent -- SDXL ~7-9 is the standard CFG-guidance band, whereas distilled / guidance-distilled models (FLUX, Qwen-Image, Z-Image-class) use a much lower 'guidance' value and break if given SDXL-range CFG. These are well-established practitioner facts consistent with the cited theory. CONFIRMED.
- **Sources:** [Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Ho, Salimans, 2022) — Guidance scale interpolates conditional vs unconditional predictions; higher scale increases adherence to the conditioning (prompt) at the cost of diversity. arXiv:2207.12598 ; [High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752) (Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser, Ommer, 2022) — Text conditioning enters the denoising UNet via cross-attention; the prompt steers the latent denoising independently of the initial noise seed. arXiv:2112.10752

### Exact reproducibility requires the WHOLE stack to match,… · `recommended` · community-claim

**Exact reproducibility requires the WHOLE stack to match, not just the seed: same model, sampler, steps, CFG, resolution, scheduler, AND node graph — plus same GPU architecture and library versions for bit-exactness.**

The seed is one of ~6 generation parameters; change any of model/sampler/steps/CFG/resolution and the image changes despite the seed. Bit-exact reproduction additionally needs matching hardware: different GPU architectures (e.g. Pascal vs Turing) 'deviate a lot' on both noise generation and downstream compute, and non-deterministic kernels (xformers/CUTLASS) break determinism even within one machine. So 'I used the same seed' guarantees nothing on its own.  [grounding: strong-community]

- **For the pipeline:** To reliably re-generate a hero asset, archive the FULL recipe: model hash + sampler + steps + CFG + resolution + scheduler + the exact node graph/workflow JSON + seed (and note the GPU). Store the ComfyUI workflow embedded in the PNG. Do NOT expect to reproduce a shot from the seed alone, and don't expect bit-identical output across machines or after a library upgrade. For a commercial pipeline, pin the workflow file as the source of truth, with the seed as just one field in it.
